title: What Small Businesses Can Learn From Corporate Benefits Managers
description: What a Benefits Manager Does — and Why Small Business Owners End Up Doing the Job Themselves

blocks.text: What a Benefits Manager Does — and Why Small Business Owners End Up Doing the Job Themselves

In a large company, employee benefits are usually handled by people whose full-time job is managing employee benefits. There may be a benefits manager, HR generalist, payroll team, benefits administration platform, compliance vendor, COBRA vendor, insurance broker, and legal support.
In a small business, those same jobs often fall on the owner, office manager, bookkeeper, or payroll person.

That is one reason health insurance feels so messy for small employers. The issue is not only the cost of the plan. It is the work around the plan: choosing coverage, explaining it to employees, tracking eligibility, handling payroll deductions, reviewing invoices, distributing notices, dealing with terminations, and answering employee questions.
Large companies have a benefits department. Small businesses often have onw person wearing eight other hats.
For small businesses, understanding this gap matters. A small employer may not need a full benefits department, but it does need a clean benefits process.
What Does a Corporate Benefits Manager Actually Do?

A corporate benefits manager helps run the company’s employee benefits program. That may include health insurance, dental, vision, life insurance, disability, retirement plans, leave programs, wellness tools, voluntary benefits, and employee communication.
For this article, let’s focus mostly on health and employee benefits.
In a larger company, the benefits manager may be responsible for:
Reviewing renewal options
Comparing carriers and plan designs
Managing open enrollment
Coordinating payroll deductions
Tracking eligibility
Handling employee benefit questions
Working with vendors
Managing compliance notices
Monitoring plan documents
Reviewing invoices and enrollments
Helping leadership understand cost and employee impact
That is a lot of work. And the work does not disappear just because the company is small. It only gets pushed onto someone else.
The Small Business Version of the Same Job
A small business owner may think: “We just need health insurance.”

But once the plan is in place, the employer has to administer it. Someone has to know when new hires become eligible. Someone has to collect enrollments. Someone has to make sure payroll deductions start correctly. Someone has to remove terminated employees. Someone has to check whether the carrier invoice matches the actual employee roster.
Someone also has to answer questions like:

“Is my doctor in network?”
“Why did my prescription cost more?”
“When will I get my ID card?”
“Can I add my spouse?”
“What happens if I quit?”
“Why is my deduction different this paycheck?”

In a large company, those questions usually go to HR or benefits staff. In a small company, they often go directly to the owner. That is where benefits administration starts to feel like a part-time job.
Plan Selection and Renewal Review
One major responsibility of a benefits manager is reviewing the health plan renewal. A good renewal review is not just asking, “What is the new rate?”

It should look at the premium increase, plan design, provider network, prescription drug coverage, employer contribution, employee payroll deductions, and whether alternatives should be compared. For a small business, this often happens under pressure. The renewal arrives, the increase is uncomfortable, and the owner has to decide whether to absorb the cost, change plans, shift more cost to employees, or compare fully insured and level-funded options.
That decision affects the company’s budget and the employee experience. The smaller the company, the more personal the decision can feel.

If a 20-person company changes networks and three employees lose doctors, the owner may hear about it quickly. If the company raises employee deductions too much, employees may see it as a pay cut. That is why health plan review should be treated as a business decision, not just an annual insurance quote.
Enrollment and Employee Communication

A benefits manager also handles employee communication. This includes open enrollment materials, plan summaries, enrollment deadlines, employee meetings, plan comparisons, and basic education about deductibles, copays, networks, and prescription coverage. For small businesses, this is often one of the weakest areas.

The owner or office manager forwards a carrier PDF and hopes employees understand it. That usually is not enough. Employees may not understand the difference between a PPO and an HMO. They may not know what a deductible means. They may not understand why the cheapest plan might have a smaller network or higher out-of-pocket risk.
Good communication does not need to be fancy. It does need to be clear. At minimum, employees should understand:

What plans are available.
What the employer is contributing.
What employees will pay.
How the network works.
What the deductible and out-of-pocket maximum mean.
What the deadline is.
Who to contact with questions.
Eligibility, Waiting Periods, and Payroll Deductions

Benefits administration also means tracking who is eligible and when. This includes new hires, full-time status, waiting periods, dependent eligibility, qualifying life events, terminations, and employee waivers. It also connects directly to payroll.

If a new employee becomes eligible on the first of the month, payroll deductions need to start correctly. If someone terminates, deductions need to stop and the carrier needs to be updated. If an employee changes coverage because of marriage, birth, divorce, or loss of other coverage, the paperwork has to match the payroll changes.

This sounds simple until the company is busy. Then mistakes happen. A person gets added late. A payroll deduction is missed. A terminated employee remains on the invoice. The carrier bill does not match payroll. An employee thinks they enrolled, but the enrollment was never submitted.
These are not always huge problems, but they create unnecessary stress. A clean benefits process should connect enrollment, payroll, carrier billing, and employee communication.
Compliance and Notices

Employee benefits come with compliance responsibilities. ERISA sets minimum standards for most private-sector employer health plans and includes responsibilities for those who manage employee benefit plans. The Department of Labor explains that group health plan administration requires specific actions and responsibilities, including a written plan, recordkeeping, and documents that provide plan information to employees and the government.

Employers may also need to think about items such as summary plan descriptions, summaries of benefits and coverage, Section 125 cafeteria plan documents, COBRA or state continuation, ACA reporting, PCORI fees for some self-funded plans, and other notices depending on the situation.

COBRA is one example. The Department of Labor explains that COBRA generally applies to private-sector group health plans maintained by employers with at least 20 employees on more than 50 percent of typical business days in the prior calendar year. The same DOL guide notes that many employers hire third-party administrators, but COBRA compliance remains the employer’s responsibility under ERISA.

Small employers under the federal COBRA threshold may still have state continuation rules, depending on the state and carrier arrangement. That is one reason this area should not be guessed at. The article is not legal advice. The practical point is simple: Small businesses should not assume benefits compliance is handled automatically just because they bought insurance.
Employee Problem Solving

A benefits manager also helps employees when things go wrong. That may involve ID card issues, provider lookup, claim questions, pharmacy problems, enrollment errors, billing questions, and confusion about deductibles or copays. In a small business, this is where the owner can get pulled into time-consuming work.

An employee may ask why a claim was denied. Another may ask why a doctor says they are out of network. Another may ask why a child was not added correctly. Another may need help after a termination or qualifying life event. The owner usually should not be handling private medical details. But the employer still needs a process for helping employees find the right place to get answers.

That might mean directing the employee to the carrier, broker, enrollment platform, payroll provider, COBRA vendor, or benefits administrator. The key is having a clear path. Without one, every benefits question becomes a custom fire drill.
Strategy: The Part Small Businesses Often Miss

Large-company benefits teams usually connect benefits to business strategy. They ask how benefits affect recruiting, retention, compensation, employee satisfaction, and budget planning. Small businesses often do not get that far. They are just trying to survive the renewal.

That is understandable, but it can lead to poor decisions. For example, a small employer may choose the cheapest plan and then discover employees cannot use the network. Another may keep an expensive PPO for years without checking whether an HMO plus PPO buy-up strategy would work better. Another may accept fully insured renewals without comparing level-funded options. Benefits strategy does not have to be complicated.
It starts with a few practical questions:

Are we using benefits to help recruit and retain employees?
Are employees using and valuing the plan?
Are we paying for network access employees actually need?
Is our contribution strategy helping or hurting participation?
Are we reviewing alternatives early enough?
Are we administering the plan cleanly?
What Should a Small Business Owner Actually Do?

A small business owner does not need to personally become a benefits manager. In fact, that is usually not the best use of the owner’s time. The better approach is to build a simple process and use the right outside support.
That may include:

A broker or consultant to help compare plans and funding options.
A payroll provider to handle deductions correctly.
A benefits administration platform to manage enrollments.
A COBRA or state continuation vendor when needed.
A Section 125 or compliance vendor for plan documents and notices.
A carrier contact or service team for claim and ID card issues.
A clear internal person who coordinates the moving parts.
The small business does not need to do everything in-house. But someone needs to own the process.
Where an Advisor Should Help — and Where Vendors May Be Better

A benefits advisor should not necessarily become the company’s HR department. Some work is better handled by specialized vendors. COBRA administration, Section 125 documents, benefits administration software, ACA reporting, and payroll integration may be better outsourced to companies that do that work every day.

A good advisor can still add value by helping the owner understand what needs to be handled, which vendors may be needed, and how the pieces fit together. That is a very different role from doing every administrative task personally. For a small business, the goal should be: Get the right process, the right vendors, and the right advisory support without turning benefits into chaos.
A Simple Example
Imagine a 28-person contractor in Texas offering health insurance for the first time. The owner thinks the main decision is which plan to buy.

But once the plan is selected, the company still has to decide who is eligible, how much the company will contribute, when employees can enroll, how payroll deductions will work, who will submit enrollments, how waivers will be tracked, how ID cards will be handled, and who employees should contact with questions.
If that process is not set up clearly, the first 60 days can become messy.
Now compare that to a cleaner setup.

The employer has a simple employee census, a contribution strategy, an enrollment guide, a clear deadline, payroll deduction instructions, carrier enrollment confirmation, a COBRA or continuation process if needed, and a first-invoice review.
The plan may be the same. The experience is not. That is the difference benefits administration makes.
The Bottom Line

A corporate benefits manager does much more than pick a health insurance plan. They review renewals, manage enrollment, coordinate payroll deductions, track eligibility, communicate with employees, handle compliance tasks, work with vendors, and help leadership connect benefits to business strategy.

Small business owners often end up doing parts of that same job without realizing it. That does not mean a small business needs a full benefits department. It means the business needs a clean process and the right support. For small businesses, employee benefits should not be handled as a once-a-year scramble.
A better approach is to build a simple system:

Choose the right plan.
Explain it clearly.
Enroll employees correctly.
Connect payroll and billing.
Use vendors where needed.
Review the strategy before renewal panic sets in.
That is how small businesses can make benefits feel less chaotic and more useful.
FAQ SECTION
1. What does a benefits manager do?

A benefits manager helps run employee benefit programs. This may include plan review, open enrollment, employee communication, vendor coordination, payroll deductions, compliance support, and employee benefit questions.
2. Why does health insurance administration feel hard for small businesses?

Small businesses often do the same basic benefits work as larger companies, but without a benefits department. The owner, office manager, bookkeeper, or payroll person may have to coordinate everything.
3. Does buying health insurance automatically handle benefits compliance?

No. Buying insurance does not automatically handle every employer responsibility. ERISA-covered group health plans involve plan documents, recordkeeping, participant information, and fiduciary responsibilities.
4. Does every small business have to offer health insurance?

Small employers generally have different ACA rules than large employers. HealthCare.gov describes SHOP coverage as generally available to small employers with 1–50 employees, and the IRS notes that some ACA provisions apply to small employers generally with fewer than 50 full-time employees, including full-time equivalents.
5. Who handles COBRA for small businesses?

Federal COBRA generally applies to private-sector group health plans maintained by employers with at least 20 employees, but many employers use third-party administrators. State continuation rules may apply to smaller employers depending on the state.
6. Should a small business outsource benefits administration?
Often, yes. Payroll deductions, COBRA, Section 125 documents, enrollment platforms, ACA reporting, and compliance notices may be better handled by specialized vendors.
7. What is the biggest benefits administration mistake small employers make?
One common mistake is treating benefits as only a renewal decision. The plan also needs enrollment, payroll coordination, employee communication, invoice review, and ongoing administration.

title: Why Lower Health Premiums Are Not Always Better
description: When a small business gets a health insurance renewal, the first number everyone looks at is the premium.

blocks.text: When a small business gets a health insurance renewal, the first number everyone looks at is the premium.

The premium is easy to compare. One plan costs $8,000 per month. Another costs $7,200. A third costs $6,900. When health insurance is already one of the company’s biggest expenses, the lower number gets attention fast. But, a lower premium does not always mean a better plan.

Sometimes the lower-cost plan is a smart move. Other times, the lower premium is hiding a tradeoff that will show up later through higher employee costs, a weaker provider network, prescription drug problems, more administrative work, or a plan structure that is not a good fit for the company.

For small businesses, the goal should not be to buy the cheapest health plan. The goal should be to buy the plan that gives the best balance of cost, employee access, risk protection, and long-term fit. That requires looking past the premium.
Why the Lowest Premium Is So Tempting
Small employers are under real pressure.

KFF’s 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey found that the average annual premium for employer-sponsored family coverage reached $26,993 in 2025. The same survey reported an average annual deductible of $1,886 for single coverage among covered workers in plans with a general annual deductible. Those numbers help explain why owners focus so heavily on cost.

If a lower-premium plan appears to save the company thousands of dollars per year, it deserves attention. The mistake is assuming that lower premium automatically means better value. Health insurance cost can move from one place to another. A plan may lower the monthly premium by increasing deductibles, limiting the network, changing prescription drug coverage, increasing employee cost-sharing, or shifting more risk to the employer.
That may still be acceptable. But the business owner should understand the tradeoff before making the change.
Premium Is Only One Part of the Cost
A health plan has several different cost layers.

The employer pays premium. Employees may pay part of the premium through payroll deductions. Employees also pay out-of-pocket costs when they use care, such as deductibles, copays, and coinsurance. Healthcare.gov explains that out-of-pocket costs include deductibles, coinsurance, copayments, and costs for services not covered by the plan.

That means a plan with a lower premium may still cost employees more when they actually use healthcare. A deductible is the amount a person pays for covered healthcare services before the plan starts paying. Healthcare.gov gives the example of a $2,000 deductible, where the person pays the first $2,000 of covered services before the plan begins paying according to the plan rules. For a business owner, this matters because employees often judge the plan by what happens when they need care. A lower premium may help the company budget, but employees may feel worse off if they face higher costs at the doctor, hospital, pharmacy, or specialist.
A Cheap Plan Can Become Expensive for Employees

A lower-premium plan may look good in the employer budget but create problems for employees. For example, a company may move from a plan with a $1,500 deductible to a plan with a $5,000 deductible. The premium goes down. The employer saves money. But employees who use the plan may now feel like the coverage does not help until they spend thousands of dollars. That can hurt morale.

This is especially important for small businesses because benefits are personal. In a large company, employees may complain to HR. In a small company, they may complain directly to the owner, office manager, or supervisor. The lower-cost plan may still be the right choice. But the employer should know whether the savings come from real efficiency or from shifting more cost to employees.
The Network May Be Smaller

Provider network is one of the biggest places where lower premiums can hide tradeoffs. A plan may cost less because it uses a smaller network, an HMO, an EPO, or a more focused group of doctors and hospitals. That can be a good cost-control strategy if the network fits the employees. But if employees lose access to their doctors, hospitals, specialists, pediatricians, or mental health providers, the lower premium may create frustration quickly.

This is not a reason to avoid smaller networks. In fact, a smaller network can be a smart choice if it includes the providers employees actually use. It may even be possible to offer a lower-cost HMO as the base plan and a broader PPO as a buy-up option.

A small employer should check whether the lower-cost network works where employees live and seek care. A doctor match review can help. That means checking whether employees’ important providers are included in the lower-cost network before making the switch.
For small employers, this can be a real advantage. A 20-person company may be able to do a practical provider check in a way a 2,000-person company cannot.
Prescription Drug Coverage May Change

Prescription drug coverage is another area where a lower-premium plan may create problems. Two plans may both say they cover prescriptions. But that does not mean they cover them the same way. One plan may have lower copays for generics but higher costs for brand-name drugs. Another may place more medications on higher tiers. Another may require prior authorization before certain drugs are approved. Specialty drugs may have separate rules or cost-sharing.

KFF’s 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey notes that employer plans commonly use prescription drug formularies, cost-sharing tiers, and other tools to manage prescription coverage. For employees who take only low-cost generics, the change may not matter much. For employees using brand-name drugs, specialty drugs, or medications with special approval rules, the difference can be significant.

A small employer usually does not need to become a pharmacy expert. But before choosing a lower-premium plan, someone should review how the prescription drug coverage changes. Otherwise, the company may save money on premium and create a new problem at the pharmacy counter.
The Out-of-Pocket Maximum Matters

The out-of-pocket maximum is another important number. Healthcare.gov defines the out-of-pocket maximum as the most a person has to pay for covered services in a plan year. For 2026 Marketplace plans, Healthcare.gov lists the maximum as $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family.

Employer plans can vary, but the concept matters in every plan comparison. A lower-premium plan may come with a higher out-of-pocket maximum. That may not matter to an employee who barely uses care. It can matter a lot to an employee who has surgery, a serious illness, a complicated pregnancy, cancer treatment, or a major accident.

The employer should understand the worst-case employee exposure before choosing a cheaper plan. A plan is not automatically bad because the out-of-pocket maximum is higher. But the employer should know who is carrying more of the risk.
Lower Premium Can Mean More Employee Confusion

Cheaper plans are sometimes more complicated. That may happen because of network rules, referral rules, prior authorization, pharmacy restrictions, separate specialty drug rules, or unfamiliar plan structures. A broad PPO may be expensive, but employees usually understand it. A lower-cost HMO, EPO, reference-based pricing plan, or level-funded plan may require more explanation.

That does not make those options wrong. Some of them can be very good. But if employees do not understand how to use the plan, the employer may face problems. Employees may go out of network by mistake, skip care, get surprised by bills, or blame the company when the issue is really plan design.
A lower premium is not worth much if employees cannot figure out how to use the coverage.
Fully Insured vs. Level-Funded: Cheaper Quotes Need a Careful Review
Level-funded plans can be attractive for small employers, especially groups with favorable demographics or lower expected claims.

They may offer a lower monthly cost, more claims visibility, and sometimes the possibility of a surplus refund if claims come in lower than expected. KFF describes level-funded arrangements as self-funded-style plans packaged with stop-loss coverage, and KFF reported that in 2025, 37% of covered workers in firms with 10 to 199 workers were enrolled in a level-funded plan. That is important. Level funding is no longer some obscure concept. It is a major part of the small-employer market.

But a lower level-funded quote should still be reviewed carefully. The employer should understand the network, prescription drug program, stop-loss protection, maximum claim exposure, renewal process, surplus refund rules, and what happens if claims are higher than expected.

A level-funded plan may be the better choice. It may also be the wrong fit if the employer wants maximum simplicity or cannot handle the added complexity. A lower quote is only useful if the structure behind it makes sense.
A Simple Example
Imagine a 24-person contractor in Texas.
The company’s current health plan renews at $18,000 per month. A new plan is offered at $15,500 per month. On the surface, the savings look excellent.

But after reviewing the details, the employer learns that the lower-cost plan has a smaller network, higher prescription drug costs for some brand-name medications, and a higher out-of-pocket maximum.

That does not automatically make the cheaper plan bad. It may still be the right move if employees’ doctors are in network, most employees use low-cost prescriptions, and the company communicates the changes clearly. But if several employees lose important providers and a few face much higher drug costs, the cheaper plan may create more problems than it solves. The premium savings need to be compared against the full impact.
When the Lower-Cost Plan May Be the Right Choice

Sometimes the cheaper plan really is the better plan. That may happen when the lower premium comes from a more efficient network, a smarter funding structure, better plan design, or a contribution strategy that fits the workforce.

For example, a company may offer a lower-cost HMO as the base plan and contribute heavily toward it. Employees who want broader access can buy up to a PPO. That can lower company costs while still giving employees a choice. A lower-premium plan may also work well when employees are young, local, comfortable with the network, and not heavily tied to specific providers.
The point is not to avoid cheap plans. The point is to understand why the plan is cheaper.
When the Lower-Cost Plan May Be a Problem

A lower-cost plan deserves more caution when the savings come mostly from shifting risk or disruption to employees. Warning signs include a much smaller network, major increases in deductibles or out-of-pocket maximums, weaker prescription drug coverage, unclear specialty drug rules, no good employee support, or plan terms the employer does not fully understand.

Another warning sign is speed. If the employer is making the decision at the last minute, there may not be enough time to review provider networks, drug coverage, payroll deductions, employee communication, or enrollment setup. A cheap plan chosen in a rush can become expensive in employee frustration.
How Small Employers Should Compare Plans

A good comparison should look beyond premium. The employer should review the network, employee providers, deductibles, copays, coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximums, prescription drug rules, contribution strategy, funding structure, and likely employee disruption.

The employer should also ask how the plan will feel to employees. A plan that looks strong on paper may fail if employees see it as confusing or unusable. This is where a benefits review becomes valuable. The goal is not just to quote plans. The goal is to compare tradeoffs in a way the business owner can actually use.
A cheaper plan may be better. A more expensive plan may be worth keeping. A two-option strategy may be better than either one by itself.
The Bottom Line
A lower health insurance premium can be attractive, and sometimes it is the right move. But, lower premium does not automatically mean better value.
The savings may come from a smaller network, higher employee cost-sharing, prescription drug changes, more plan complexity, or a funding structure that needs closer review.
For small businesses, the better approach is to compare the full plan, not just the rate.
A smart health insurance review should ask: What are we saving, what are we giving up, and will employees still be able to use the plan effectively?
That is the difference between buying the cheapest plan and building a better benefits strategy.
FAQ SECTION
1. Is the cheapest health insurance plan usually the best choice for a small business?
Not always. A lower premium may come with a smaller network, higher deductibles, higher out-of-pocket costs, prescription drug restrictions, or more employee confusion.
2. Why can a lower-premium plan cost employees more?

A lower-premium plan may shift more cost to employees through deductibles, copays, coinsurance, or higher out-of-pocket maximums. Healthcare.gov explains that out-of-pocket costs include deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance for covered services.
3. What is a deductible?

A deductible is the amount a person pays for covered healthcare services before the plan starts to pay. Healthcare.gov gives the example of a $2,000 deductible, where the person pays the first $2,000 of covered services before the plan begins paying according to the plan rules.
4. Why does the provider network matter when comparing plans?

The network affects which doctors, hospitals, and specialists employees can use. A lower-cost plan may have a smaller network, which can save money but may also create disruption if employees lose access to important providers.
5. Can prescription drug coverage be different between health plans?

Yes. Plans may use different drug tiers, formularies, prior authorization rules, preferred pharmacies, and specialty drug rules. KFF notes that employer plans commonly use formularies and cost-sharing tiers for prescription drugs.
6. Are level-funded plans always cheaper than fully insured plans?

No. Level-funded plans may be attractive for some small employers, but the employer should review the network, claims funding, stop-loss protection, prescription drug program, renewal process, and plan terms before deciding.
7. What should a small employer compare besides premium?

A good comparison should include provider network, employee provider access, deductibles, copays, coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximums, prescription coverage, employer contribution strategy, employee disruption, and funding structure.

title: Prescription Costs: What Small Businesses Can and Cannot Control
description: Prescription drug costs are one of the most frustrating parts of health insurance.

blocks.text: Prescription drug costs are one of the most frustrating parts of health insurance.
Employees feel it when they go to the pharmacy. One person may pay a small copay for a generic drug. Another may face a much higher cost for a brand-name or specialty medication.

Employers feel it differently. A small business owner may see the health insurance renewal increase and wonder how much of the increase is tied to prescriptions. But in many fully insured small-group plans, the owner does not get much detail and does not have much control over the drug program.

That is the important starting point. A small business owner can understand prescription drug costs. They can compare plans. They can ask better renewal questions. They can help employees understand how the plan works. But if the company is in a standard fully insured ACA small-group plan, the employer usually cannot rebuild the prescription drug program from scratch.

That does not make the topic useless. It makes it more important to understand. Prescription drug costs are one of the places where the difference between fully insured and level-funded health plans becomes clearer.
Why Prescription Drug Costs Matter

Prescription drugs are part of the claims cost inside a health insurance premium. Some drugs are inexpensive. Others can cost hundreds, thousands, or even tens of thousands of dollars per month. For a small company, one high-cost prescription can matter more than many routine doctor visits.

KFF’s 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey notes that nearly all covered workers are at firms that provide prescription drug coverage in their largest health plan. KFF also explains that employer plans commonly use drug formularies, cost-sharing tiers, and other tools to manage prescription coverage. That means prescription drug coverage is not one simple benefit.

A health plan may treat drugs differently depending on whether they are generic, brand-name, non-preferred, specialty, or subject to special rules. To an employee, that may feel confusing. To an employer, it matters because the drug program affects both employee experience and plan cost.
Generic, Brand, and Specialty Drugs
A simple way to understand prescription drug cost is to divide drugs into three broad categories.
Generic drugs are usually the lowest-cost option. These are medications whose patents have expired and may be made by multiple companies.
Brand-name drugs are usually more expensive. Some have generic alternatives. Others do not.

Specialty drugs are often the biggest concern for health plans. KFF describes specialty drugs as high-cost drugs that may be used for complex or chronic conditions, and they may require special handling or special pharmacy rules.

Specialty drugs are where small employers can get surprised. A company with 20 employees does not need many high-cost prescriptions to feel pressure. One specialty medication may create a large claim all by itself. That does not mean the employee is doing anything wrong. People need the medications they need. But from a plan-cost standpoint, specialty drugs can be a major driver.
GLP-1 Drugs Made This More Visible

GLP-1 drugs have made prescription drug costs a bigger topic for employers. These drugs may be used for type 2 diabetes, and some are also used for weight loss. Common examples include Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Saxenda, and similar medications.
KFF has noted that employers are paying close attention to GLP-1 coverage because of the cost of the drugs and the possibility that people may use them long term.
This does not mean GLP-1 drugs are bad. For some people, they may be very helpful. The issue for employers is different: Who pays, under what rules, and how does it affect the plan over time?
Large employers may have more data and more ability to adjust coverage strategy. Small employers in fully insured plans usually have less control.
Why Fully Insured Small Employers Have Limited Control

In a fully insured ACA small-group plan, the employer is mostly buying a finished product. The insurance carrier controls the prescription drug program. That usually includes the drug list, drug tiers, prior authorization rules, specialty pharmacy rules, and pharmacy benefit manager arrangement.

The employer can choose among available plans, but usually cannot say: “Keep this medical plan, but remove this specialty drug.” Or: “Use this carrier, but let us choose our own prescription drug manager.” That is usually not how fully insured small-group coverage works.

There is also an ACA issue. Non-grandfathered individual and small-group health insurance plans must cover essential health benefits, and prescription drugs are one of the required essential health benefit categories. So in fully insured small-group coverage, the employer can usually choose between available drug programs. The employer usually cannot redesign the drug program.
What Is a PBM?
A pharmacy benefit manager, often called a PBM, is a company that helps run the prescription drug part of a health plan.

The PBM may help decide which drugs are covered, which drugs are preferred, what employees pay at the pharmacy, whether prior authorization is required, and which pharmacies employees can use. NAIC describes PBMs as third-party companies that act as intermediaries between insurance carriers and pharmaceutical manufacturers. NAIC also notes that PBMs may create formularies, negotiate rebates, process claims, create pharmacy networks, review drug use, and manage mail-order or specialty pharmacies. In a fully insured small-group plan, the employer usually does not choose the PBM directly. The carrier has already built the prescription drug program into the plan.
That is why small employers often have limited control. They are not managing the drug program themselves. They are choosing from the drug programs attached to the plans available in their market.
Why Fully Insured Plans Can Feel Disconnected From Your Own Drug Costs

In a fully insured small-group plan, your premium is not based only on your own company’s prescription drug use. You are buying into a larger insurance pool. That pool includes many employers and many employees. Some may use very few prescriptions. Others may use expensive brand-name drugs, specialty medications, or long-term therapies. That pooling is part of what makes fully insured coverage stable. If one of your employees suddenly needs a very expensive medication, the carrier takes on that risk. Your company is not directly paying that claim out of pocket.
But there is a tradeoff.

If your group has low prescription drug use, you usually do not get a direct reward for that. You are still paying into a premium structure that reflects the carrier’s broader expected drug costs. This is one reason some healthier or lower-claim small businesses compare level-funded plans.

In a level-funded arrangement, the employer’s cost may be more closely connected to its own group’s expected and actual claims experience. That can help some groups, especially if their own risk profile is better than the broader small-group pool.
But this needs to be said clearly: Level funding does not eliminate prescription drug risk.

If someone is already using a high-cost drug, that may affect the quote. If someone starts using one later, that may affect claims or future pricing. Level funding may offer more visibility and more tools. It is not a magic way to avoid all future drug costs.
What Small Employers Can Still Do in Fully Insured Plans
Even with limited control, small employers are not helpless.

The first step is to compare available plans. Different carriers and plans may handle prescriptions differently. One plan may have lower copays but a higher premium. Another may have a deductible that applies before drug coverage begins. Another may place specialty drugs on a separate tier.

The second step is to understand how employees are likely to experience the drug benefit. Are common medications easy to fill? Are specialty drugs handled through a specialty pharmacy? Are prior authorizations required? Are there preferred pharmacies or mail-order options?

The third step is employee education. Employees should know how to ask doctors about generic alternatives, preferred drugs, and lower-cost options. They should also understand that using a discount card outside the plan may not count toward their deductible or out-of-pocket maximum.
These steps may not transform the employer’s premium. But they can reduce confusion and help employees use the plan better.
Where Level-Funded and Self-Funded Plans May Offer More Control

The bigger change happens when an employer moves away from a standard fully insured plan. In a level-funded or self-funded plan, the employer may have more flexibility, depending on the carrier, third-party administrator, PBM, stop-loss carrier, and plan design.

KFF describes level-funded arrangements as self-funded-style plans packaged with stop-loss coverage, where the employer typically pays a set monthly amount that includes expected claims, administrative fees, and stop-loss protection. KFF also reported that in 2025, 37% of covered workers in firms with 10 to 199 workers were enrolled in a level-funded plan.

This matters because the employer may no longer be buying the same kind of pooled, fully insured drug program. The plan may be priced more closely around the group’s own expected risk and claims experience. That can help some small businesses. It may also create more room to use prescription drug cost-control tools.

Those tools may include stronger specialty drug management, more transparent PBM arrangements, different formulary strategies, prior authorization rules, step therapy, site-of-care management for infused drugs, or specialty pharmacy programs.

Some plans may also explore specialty drug carve-outs or alternative funding strategies. But more control also means more responsibility. A plan that aggressively manages prescription drugs may lower costs, but it can also create employee confusion, access concerns, or administrative problems if it is not handled well.
Specialty Drug Carve-Outs Need Careful Review

A specialty drug carve-out means certain high-cost drugs are handled differently from the standard prescription drug program. That may sound attractive. If a category of drugs is driving cost, why not manage it separately? Sometimes that may be worth reviewing. But it is not a simple fix.

A carve-out can create legal, administrative, and employee experience issues. The plan document must be clear. Claims and appeals rules matter. Employees need to understand what is covered and what process they need to follow.

ERISA also matters. The Department of Labor explains that ERISA sets standards for people who manage employee benefit plans and that an ERISA-covered group health plan can include prescription drug coverage. So the message should not be: “Carve out specialty drugs and save money.” A better message is: “Some level-funded or self-funded plans may offer more prescription drug cost-control tools, but those tools need careful review.”
PBMs, Rebates, and Why This Gets Complicated

Prescription drug pricing can be hard to see clearly. The price paid at the pharmacy, the rebate from the drug manufacturer, the employee’s copay, and the plan’s net cost may all be different numbers. PBMs are part of that system. They may negotiate rebates, build formularies, process claims, and manage pharmacy networks.

In a fully insured small-group plan, the employer usually has limited visibility into this system. In a self-funded or level-funded plan, the employer may get more information. But that depends on the plan, PBM, carrier, administrator, and reporting. This is why prescription drug strategy is not just about telling employees to choose cheaper drugs. It is also about plan structure, transparency, and administration.
A Simple Example
Imagine a 25-person professional firm in Illinois.

The company has a fully insured small-group health plan. One employee uses a specialty medication. Another employee is interested in a GLP-1 medication. The owner sees the renewal increase and wonders whether prescriptions are part of the problem. In the fully insured plan, the owner probably cannot remove a drug category, change the PBM, or redesign the specialty drug program. The owner can compare available plans and review how each handles prescriptions.
Now imagine the firm also reviews a level-funded option.

That option may provide more visibility and more prescription drug management tools. It may have stronger rules around specialty drugs, prior authorization, preferred pharmacies, or site-of-care management. It may also come with more complexity.

Neither option is automatically better. The fully insured plan may be simpler and more familiar. The level-funded plan may offer more control and may better reflect the group’s own risk. The best fit depends on the employer’s workforce, risk tolerance, claims profile, and need for predictability.
The Bottom Line

Prescription drug costs are an important part of health insurance premiums. Some prescriptions are inexpensive. Others, especially specialty drugs and certain newer therapies, can create major cost pressure. For fully insured small-group plans, small employers usually have limited control. They can compare carriers and plan designs, but they generally cannot rebuild the drug program. They are also paying into a broader insurance pool. That gives them protection if one of their own employees needs an expensive medication, but it also means they may be paying for broader expected drug costs even when their own group has low drug use.

Level-funded and self-funded plans may offer more tools. These can include specialty drug management, PBM transparency, prior authorization, site-of-care rules, and sometimes specialty carve-out strategies. But those tools require careful review, good administration, and clear employee communication.

For small businesses, the right approach is not to chase every aggressive cost-control idea. The right approach is to understand what the current plan allows, what alternatives are available, and whether more control is worth the added complexity.
FAQ SECTION
1. Do prescription drugs affect small business health insurance premiums?
Yes. Prescription drugs are part of the claims cost inside a health plan. High-cost specialty drugs can create meaningful pressure on plan costs, especially for small groups.
2. Can a small employer control prescription costs in a fully insured plan?

Only in limited ways. A small employer can compare available carriers and plan designs, but the carrier usually controls the formulary, PBM, drug tiers, prior authorization rules, and specialty pharmacy rules.
3. Are prescription drugs required in ACA small-group plans?
Yes. Non-grandfathered individual and small-group health insurance plans must cover essential health benefits, and prescription drugs are one of the required benefit categories.
4. What is a PBM?

A PBM, or pharmacy benefit manager, helps manage the prescription drug part of a health plan. PBMs may create formularies, process claims, negotiate rebates, create pharmacy networks, and manage specialty or mail-order pharmacy programs.
5. What are specialty drugs?
Specialty drugs are high-cost medications often used for complex or chronic conditions. They may require special handling, special approval, or use of a specialty pharmacy.
6. Can level-funded plans offer more prescription drug control?

Sometimes. Level-funded or self-funded plans may allow more flexibility around PBM arrangements, specialty drugs, prior authorization, and other cost-control tools. The details depend on the plan, vendor, contract, and stop-loss arrangement.
7. What is a specialty drug carve-out?

A specialty drug carve-out means certain high-cost drugs are handled outside the standard drug program or managed under a separate strategy. This can create savings opportunities, but it can also create legal, administrative, and employee communication issues.
8. Should every small business try to carve out specialty drugs?
No. Specialty drug carve-outs need careful review. They may not fit every employer and should be evaluated with qualified plan, legal, and administrative guidance.

title: Can A Small Business Control What Their Health Plan Is Billed?
description: How Reference-Based Pricing Can Help Small Employers Control Health Insurance Costs

blocks.text: How Reference-Based Pricing Can Help Small Employers Control Health Insurance Costs

Most small business owners think of health insurance in terms of networks. A PPO gives employees broad access. An HMO usually limits access to a smaller network. An EPO sits somewhere in between. The insurance carrier negotiates rates with doctors and hospitals, and the employer pays the premium.
Reference-based pricing works differently.
Instead of relying only on a traditional provider network contract, a reference-based pricing plan sets a payment limit based on an outside benchmark. That benchmark is often tied to Medicare.
For example, instead of paying whatever a hospital negotiated with a commercial insurance carrier, the plan might say: “For this service, we will pay 150% of Medicare.”
That sounds simple. It can be powerful. It can also create real problems if employees are not supported properly.

Reference-based pricing, often shortened to RBP, is not usually something a small business buys as a standard fully insured ACA small-group plan. It is more commonly used inside a self-funded or level-funded employer health plan, where the employer has more control over how claims are paid.
For the right employer, RBP can be a serious cost-control strategy. For the wrong employer, it can create employee confusion, provider pushback, and billing disputes.
The value comes from understanding both sides before making the move.
What Is Reference-Based Pricing?

Reference-based pricing is a health plan payment method that uses a benchmark to decide how much the plan will pay for certain healthcare services. Nationwide describes reference-based pricing as a plan design that uses Medicare reimbursement rates, or a derived equivalent, as a reference point and prices claims based on a multiple of that rate.
In plain English, the plan does not start with the hospital’s billed charge. It does not necessarily start with a traditional PPO discount either. It starts with a reference point.
That reference point might be Medicare, a percentage above Medicare, another published pricing benchmark, or a direct contract with certain providers.
The most common way to explain it is: Medicare plus a percentage.
For example, a plan might pay a hospital claim at 140%, 150%, or 180% of Medicare. The exact percentage depends on the plan design, vendor, service type, market, and employer strategy.
The goal is not to underpay providers or create conflict. The goal is to avoid paying open-ended commercial prices that may be far above a more transparent benchmark.
Why Employers Look at Reference-Based Pricing

Employers look at RBP because commercial healthcare prices can be much higher than Medicare-based prices. RAND’s 2024 Hospital Price Transparency Study found that employers and private insurers paid hospitals an average of about 254% of what Medicare would have paid for the same inpatient and outpatient services in 2022, with wide variation by state and hospital.
That does not mean Medicare always pays the “right” amount. It also does not mean every hospital is doing something wrong.
It does show why employers are frustrated.

If a small business is paying premiums based on commercial hospital prices, and those prices are often two to three times Medicare, the owner may reasonably want a more disciplined way to pay for care. Reference-based pricing is one way to approach that problem.
A Simple Example
Assume an employee needs an outpatient procedure and the hospital’s billed charge is $12,000.

Here is how payment might look under different arrangements (these numbers are only illustrative). Maybe; Medicare pays $3,000, a PPO pays $7,620 and RBP pays $4,500.  It's only an example but it shows the basic idea.

The RBP plan is not saying it will pay nothing. It is saying it will pay based on a transparent reference point instead of simply accepting a higher commercial network price. If this happens across enough hospital and facility claims, the savings can be meaningful.
How Reference-Based Pricing Controls Costs
Reference-based pricing controls costs by changing the starting point for payment.

In a traditional PPO arrangement, the employer often sees the negotiated discount but may not know whether the final allowed amount is actually reasonable. A 40% discount sounds good, but if the starting charge is very high, the final price may still be expensive.
RBP tries to avoid that problem by using a clearer benchmark.
Instead of asking whether the plan received a discount off a hospital’s billed charge, RBP asks how the payment compares to a known reference point. That can help control costs in several ways.

It creates a clearer ceiling on certain claims. It makes the pricing logic easier to explain. It may also reduce the plan’s exposure to extremely high facility prices, especially for hospital-based care.
This is why RBP is most often discussed around hospital and facility claims. That is where commercial prices can vary widely and where employer-sponsored plans may pay much more than Medicare.
How Doctors and Hospitals Get Paid Under RBP

In a traditional PPO plan, the provider has a contract with the insurance network. The provider agrees to accept the negotiated allowed amount, and the employee pays the plan’s normal cost-sharing. Reference-based pricing may work differently.

If there is no network contract with the provider, the plan pays the claim according to its reference-based pricing formula. The provider may accept the payment. Or the provider may object and try to bill the employee for the difference between the billed charge and what the plan paid.
That difference is often called a balance bill.
This is the biggest practical issue with RBP.

A good RBP program needs more than a pricing formula. It needs member support, provider communication, claim negotiation, legal support where appropriate, and a clear process for handling provider disputes. Without that support, employees may feel caught between the health plan and the provider.
The Main Problem: Balance Billing Risk

Reference-based pricing can reduce plan costs, but it can also increase the chance of billing disputes. If a provider does not have a contract requiring it to accept the plan’s payment amount, the provider may bill the employee for the remaining balance.

The federal No Surprises Act protects patients from many surprise bills in emergency situations and certain non-emergency situations involving out-of-network providers at in-network facilities. CMS describes the law as providing protections against surprise billing and a process for resolving out-of-network payment disputes between providers and health plans.
Those protections are important, but they do not eliminate every possible billing dispute.

For example, if an employee voluntarily uses a non-contracted provider for a planned service, and that service is not protected by the No Surprises Act or another applicable law, there may still be billing risk. So RBP should not be presented as “use any provider and everything will be fine.” A more honest explanation is: Reference-based pricing can control costs, but it needs a strong process to protect employees from confusion and billing disputes.
Why Employee Education Matters
RBP can fail if employees do not understand how to use the plan.

In a PPO, employees are used to asking whether a provider is in network. In an RBP plan, the process may be different. Employees may need to contact the plan before scheduled procedures, confirm how the claim will be handled, and know what to do if a provider sends a balance bill.

That is a big change. Employees need clear instructions before elective procedures, imaging, surgeries, or hospital-based care. They should know who to call, how to confirm provider acceptance, and what to do if they receive a confusing bill.

A strong RBP strategy should include clear employee materials, a member advocacy team, help before scheduled procedures, support with balance bills, and a process for negotiating disputed claims. The plan design is only part of the solution. The service model matters just as much.
Why RBP Usually Comes Through ERISA, Self-Funded, or Level-Funded Plans

Reference-based pricing is not usually offered as a typical fully insured ACA small-group product. A fully insured small-group plan is an insurance policy issued by a carrier. The employer pays a premium, and the insurer takes the claims risk.

RBP is more commonly used in self-funded health plans. KFF explains that self-funded plans are generally regulated under federal law and are largely not required to comply with state insurance laws that apply to fully insured coverage.

ERISA is the federal law that sets minimum standards for most private-sector employer health plans. The Department of Labor explains that ERISA requires plans to provide plan information, includes fiduciary responsibilities, requires a claims and appeals process, and gives participants rights to sue for benefits and fiduciary breaches.

This matters because a self-funded ERISA plan gives the employer more flexibility in plan design than a standard fully insured ACA small-group policy. That does not mean the ACA disappears. Many federal requirements still apply to self-funded plans. But the structure is different from buying a fully insured small-group insurance policy.
For small employers, the most realistic access point is often level funding.
How Small Businesses Can Access RBP Through Level-Funded Plans
Level-funded plans are designed to feel more predictable than traditional self-funding while still being built on a self-funded structure.

KFF describes level-funded arrangements as nominally self-funded options that package a self-funded plan with extensive stop-loss coverage. The employer pays a set monthly amount that typically includes expected claims, administrative fees, and stop-loss protection. KFF also reported that in 2025, 37% of covered workers in firms with 10 to 199 workers were enrolled in a level-funded plan.

That is important for small businesses. Historically, more advanced cost-control strategies were easier for large employers to access. Level-funded arrangements have made some self-funded tools more available to smaller employers.

A small employer may access reference-based pricing through a level-funded plan that uses an RBP payment model, a self-funded plan administered by a third-party administrator, a hybrid arrangement that uses a network for some services and RBP for others, or a cost-containment vendor layered into the plan.

Stop-loss insurance is a key part of the structure. KFF explains that stop-loss coverage limits the amount a plan sponsor must pay in claims and may apply to individual high-cost claims or total plan claims. That protection matters because small employers cannot afford unlimited claims exposure.
RBP vs. PPO: The Tradeoff
A PPO plan gives employees familiarity. They can search a provider directory, stay in network, and usually avoid most balance-billing concerns for in-network care.
Reference-based pricing may create lower claim costs, especially on hospital and facility claims. But it may require more employee support and more active claim management.
This is not a simple “PPO bad, RBP good” comparison.
A PPO may be the better fit when employees need broad access, when recruiting matters heavily, or when the employer wants a more familiar health plan experience.
RBP may be worth considering when the employer wants a more aggressive cost-control strategy and has the right administrative support behind it.
What Could Go Wrong?
RBP has real drawbacks.

Employees may feel anxious if the plan does not work like a familiar PPO. Providers may push back on the payment amount, especially if it is far below their billed charge. Balance bills can create frustration even if the plan has a process for handling them.

The model can also create administrative complexity. A weak RBP vendor or poor member support can make the plan feel chaotic. That is a serious risk for a small business that does not have a large HR department.
Recruiting and retention also matter. A company competing for highly skilled employees may need to be careful before moving away from a familiar PPO-style model.
These problems do not make RBP unusable. They mean it should be handled carefully.
When Reference-Based Pricing May Make Sense

Reference-based pricing may be worth reviewing when a small business is facing repeated premium increases, has engaged ownership, and is open to a more hands-on health plan strategy. It may be especially relevant when the employer is already considering level funding and wants more transparency around claims costs.

RBP may be a poor fit when employees strongly value a traditional network, when the employer does not want to deal with billing disputes, or when the company lacks the time and support needed to explain the plan well. A business owner should not choose RBP simply because it looks cheaper on paper.
The better standard is practical fit: meaningful cost control, strong employee support, and a plan structure the employer can actually manage.
The Bottom Line
Reference-based pricing is a health plan payment strategy that uses a benchmark, often Medicare, to decide how much the plan will pay for certain healthcare services.

It can control costs by avoiding open-ended commercial pricing and tying payments to a more transparent reference point. That matters because employer-sponsored commercial plans often pay hospitals far more than Medicare-based amounts. RAND’s 2024 study found that employers and private insurers paid hospitals an average of about 254% of Medicare for the same inpatient and outpatient services in 2022.
But RBP is not simple. It can create provider disputes, employee confusion, and balance-billing risk if not managed well. It requires strong administration, clear communication, and member advocacy.

For small businesses, the most realistic way to explore reference-based pricing is usually through a self-funded or level-funded ERISA health plan, not a standard fully insured ACA small-group policy.
For the right employer, RBP can be a serious cost-control tool. For the wrong employer, it can create more frustration than savings.
The goal is not to chase the most aggressive pricing model. The goal is to choose a health plan structure that balances cost control, employee access, risk protection, and practical administration.
FAQ SECTION
1. What is reference-based pricing in health insurance?

Reference-based pricing is a payment method where a health plan sets payment amounts based on an outside benchmark, often Medicare. The plan may pay a percentage above Medicare instead of relying only on traditional PPO network rates.
2. How does reference-based pricing control costs?
It controls costs by tying payments to a benchmark rather than open-ended billed charges or higher commercial network rates. This can be especially useful for hospital and facility claims.
3. Is reference-based pricing the same as a PPO?
No. A PPO relies on negotiated provider network contracts. RBP may use a benchmark payment method and may not rely on the same kind of traditional provider network.
4. Can employees be balance billed under reference-based pricing?

Yes, balance billing can be a risk when there is no provider contract and no legal protection applies. The No Surprises Act protects consumers in many emergency and certain out-of-network situations, but it does not eliminate every possible billing dispute.
5. Is reference-based pricing available in fully insured ACA small-group plans?
Usually, no. RBP is more commonly used in self-funded or level-funded employer health plans. Fully insured ACA small-group plans are structured differently and are issued as insurance policies.
6. How can a small business access reference-based pricing?
A small business may access RBP through a level-funded or self-funded plan, often with a third-party administrator, stop-loss coverage, and a cost-containment vendor.
7. Are level-funded plans considered self-funded?

KFF describes level-funded arrangements as nominally self-funded options that package a self-funded plan with stop-loss coverage. They often involve a set monthly payment that includes expected claims, administrative fees, and stop-loss protection.
8. Is reference-based pricing a good idea for every small business?
No. RBP can lower costs, but it requires strong employee communication, billing support, and tolerance for a less traditional model. It is not a good fit for every employer.
Wondering Whether Reference-Based Pricing Fits Your Business?
Reference-based pricing can be a powerful cost-control strategy, but it is not something small employers should adopt casually.
