title: How the World Handles Health Care and Health Insurance
description: Americans often talk about health care as if there are only two choices: the U.S. private insurance system or “government-run health care.”

blocks.text: Americans often talk about health care as if there are only two choices: the U.S. private insurance system or “government-run health care.”
That is too simple.

Most wealthy countries use some mix of public funding, private doctors, private hospitals, private insurance, employer contributions, taxes, patient cost-sharing, and government rules. The difference is not whether private health care exists. It does almost everywhere. The real difference is how each country builds the floor underneath people when they get sick.

The United States has some of the strongest private insurance protections in the world for people who are already inside ACA-compliant major medical coverage. For example, Marketplace plans cannot reject someone, charge more, or refuse to cover essential health benefits because of a pre-existing condition. Medicaid and CHIP also cannot deny coverage or charge more because of a pre-existing condition.
That is a major protection.

But the U.S. also has a fragmented system where coverage depends heavily on job status, income, age, state rules, employer decisions, enrollment windows, plan networks, deductibles, and program eligibility. So the American system can be very generous once someone is in the right plan, but it does not create the same universal floor that many other countries build into their national systems.
That is the key difference.
The U.S. System: Strong Insurance Rights, Weak Universal Floor
The U.S. system is not purely private. It is a patchwork.

Some people are covered by employer-sponsored insurance. Some are covered by Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA Marketplace plans, VA coverage, TRICARE, or other public programs. Some people have no coverage at all. Others technically have coverage but still face high deductibles, narrow networks, prior authorization, pharmacy restrictions, or out-of-network costs.

This creates a strange contradiction. The U.S. has strong rules against pre-existing-condition exclusions in ACA-compliant coverage, but it still leaves people exposed to high costs and coverage gaps.

The U.S. also spends far more than other wealthy countries. OECD data for 2025 showed U.S. health spending at about $14,885 per person, compared with an OECD average of about $5,967. Health spending was about 17.2% of U.S. GDP, compared with 9.3% across the OECD.

So the issue is not that the U.S. refuses to spend money on health care. The issue is that the money moves through a complicated mix of taxes, employer premiums, employee premiums, deductibles, copays, coinsurance, public programs, subsidies, and private contracts.
In plain English: Americans pay taxes for health care, then often pay premiums, then often pay again when they use care.
Portugal: A Public Safety Net With Private Options on Top
Portugal is a good contrast.

Portugal’s public health system, the Serviço Nacional de Saúde, or SNS, is primarily tax-funded and provides universal coverage. The European Observatory describes Portugal as having a predominantly tax-based health system with universal coverage, with general practitioners acting as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care.
That means the basic question in Portugal is not usually, “Will an insurer take me with this medical condition?”
The question is more often, “Am I properly registered in the public system, and how quickly can I access the care I need?”
That is a very different structure from the U.S.

Portugal has also removed most user fees in the SNS. Since June 2022, user fees ended for almost all SNS services, remaining mainly for emergency care without prior SNS referral unless the patient is admitted afterward.

But that does not mean Portugal has unlimited care with no tradeoffs. Portugal still has access issues, wait times, referral pathways, and limits on what is fully covered. Private insurance and private care are often used for speed, convenience, specialist access, dental, vision, diagnostics, and services that people do not want to wait for in the public system.
This is one of the biggest lessons from looking internationally: universal coverage does not mean unlimited coverage.
It means there is a baseline system that does not depend on your employer, your health history, or whether you happen to be inside the right insurance contract.
Germany: Payroll-Funded Social Insurance
Germany uses a different model. It is not a British-style national health service and not an American-style employer insurance market.

Germany has mandatory health insurance with near-universal coverage. Most residents are covered through statutory health insurance funds, often called sickness funds, which are financed through compulsory wage contributions shared by employers and employees.
This model feels closer to payroll-based social insurance. Workers and employers pay into the system, and the system spreads risk across the population.

The important point is that Germany still uses insurers. It still has private-sector elements. It still has employer involvement. But it does not leave basic health coverage as a voluntary employer benefit in the same way the U.S. does.
Health care is treated more like part of the country’s social insurance structure.
The Netherlands and Switzerland: Private Insurance, But Not American-Style
The Netherlands and Switzerland are often mentioned by Americans because they use private insurance. But their private insurance systems are much more tightly regulated than the U.S. system.

In the Netherlands, everyone who lives or works there must take out standard health insurance. The government decides what the standard package covers, insurers must accept anyone who applies for the standard package, and they must charge the same premium regardless of age or health status. Additional insurance is optional, and insurers have more freedom to ask health questions or refuse applicants for those extra benefits.
That distinction matters.
The Dutch system uses private insurance companies, but the basic package functions like a heavily regulated public obligation. Insurers compete inside a government-defined framework.
That is very different from the American idea of private insurance as a contract that can vary dramatically by employer, state, network, deductible, carrier, and plan design.
Other Countries Have Limits. They Just Use Different Limits.
One mistake Americans sometimes make is assuming other countries cover everything.
They do not.
Every health system limits care in some way because no country can pay for every service, every drug, every provider, every hospital, and every treatment immediately for everyone.
The difference is how the limits show up.

In the U.S., limits often appear through insurance design: deductibles, copays, coinsurance, prior authorization, narrow networks, drug formularies, medical necessity reviews, out-of-network penalties, and plan exclusions.

In other countries, limits often appear through public budgets, referral systems, national benefit packages, waiting lists, cost-effectiveness reviews, centralized drug approval, or decisions about which services belong in the public system.

That is why a good U.S. employer plan can sometimes feel better than a public system overseas. It may offer faster access, broader specialist choice, stronger pharmacy coverage, or better dental and vision benefits.
But the tradeoff is that the U.S. does not guarantee that everyone has access to that good plan.
Other countries often provide a stronger floor, but not always the same ceiling.
The Safety Net Question: Does Covering Everyone Actually Help?
The strongest argument for universal coverage is not that it magically makes health care cheap.
It does not.
The stronger argument is that a universal safety net makes society less fragile.

When people avoid care because of cost, manageable problems can become expensive problems. KFF found that uninsured adults are much more likely than insured adults to delay or skip needed care or medication because of cost.

Medical debt is another major issue. KFF estimates that people in the United States owe at least $220 billion in medical debt, with about 14 million people owing more than $1,000 and about 3 million owing more than $10,000.
That debt does not stay neatly inside the health care system. It affects credit, savings, rent, family stress, job choices, and future care decisions.

A stronger safety net can reduce that kind of damage. It can help people treat diabetes, blood pressure, asthma, cancer, mental health conditions, pregnancy complications, and chronic illness earlier. It can also make workers less dependent on staying in a job solely because they need the health insurance.
That matters for small businesses, too.

In the U.S., small employers are often forced to compete with large employers on benefits. That is hard. Large companies usually have more HR staff, more negotiating power, more predictable risk pools, and more resources to absorb premium increases.

A universal safety net would not eliminate the need for employer benefits, but it would change what employer benefits are expected to do. Employers might still offer supplemental benefits, private access, dental, vision, disability, life insurance, executive benefits, and other perks. But they would not be carrying as much of the burden for basic medical security.
Does Universal Coverage Save Money?
Sometimes. Not automatically.

Universal coverage can create savings when it helps people get care earlier, reduces avoidable hospitalizations, lowers medical debt, simplifies administration, and gives the system enough bargaining power to control prices.

But if a country covers everyone while still paying very high prices for hospitals, drugs, specialists, administration, and billing complexity, total spending may not fall. More people using care can increase spending unless the system also controls prices and manages access.
That is why other countries use limits. They may rely on referral systems, public budgets, national fee schedules, drug reimbursement rules, or defined benefit packages.
The U.S. also uses limits. We just tend to hide them inside insurance contracts.
So the honest answer is this: universal coverage is not automatically cheaper, but it can be more stable, more predictable, and less financially destructive for families.
What the U.S. Can Learn From the Rest of the World
The U.S. does not need to pretend every other country has solved health care perfectly. They have not.

Portugal has wait times and public-system capacity issues. Canada has access delays and narrower public coverage for some services. England has budget pressure. Germany has payroll costs. The Netherlands and Switzerland still require people to pay premiums. No system escapes tradeoffs.
But other wealthy countries generally start with a different assumption.
They treat basic health coverage as a public or social obligation first, then allow private insurance or private care to sit on top of that foundation.

The U.S. often does the opposite. It starts with private coverage, employer benefits, program eligibility, and insurance contracts, then tries to patch the gaps with public programs, subsidies, hospital charity care, emergency care rules, and financial assistance.
That is why the U.S. system feels so complicated.

It is not simply private. It is not simply public. It is a very expensive hybrid that relies heavily on employers and insurance contracts to do work that other countries handle through national systems, social insurance, or tightly regulated mandatory coverage.
The Bottom Line
America is not the only country with private health care, private insurance, hospitals, specialists, networks, premiums, or patient cost-sharing.
What makes the U.S. unusual is the combination of:
employer-based coverage, high prices, fragmented public programs, private insurance complexity, no fully universal coverage guarantee, and significant out-of-pocket exposure.
Other countries have limits, too. They just deal with those limits differently.
The best way to describe the tradeoff is this:
The U.S. can provide excellent coverage for people inside the right plan, but it does not provide the same reliable floor for everyone.
Countries like Portugal provide a stronger public floor, but people may use private insurance or private care for speed, convenience, or services outside the public system.

For business owners, this matters because health care in the U.S. is not just a medical issue. It is a recruiting issue, a payroll issue, a compliance issue, a budgeting issue, and a benefits strategy issue.

That is why small employers need to understand more than just premiums. They need to understand what kind of system they are operating inside — and how to design benefits that protect employees without wasting money.

title: How Doctors and Hospitals Get Paid by Medicare, PPOs and HMOs
description: Why the Same Healthcare Service Can Cost Different Amounts in Different Health Insurance Networks

blocks.text: Why the Same Healthcare Service Can Cost Different Amounts in Different Health Insurance Networks
Most small business owners assume healthcare works like other purchases. A service has a price. The customer pays the price. The provider gets paid.

Health insurance does not work that simply. The same office visit, MRI, surgery, hospital stay, or outpatient procedure can be paid very differently depending on who is paying, which network is involved, and what contract exists between the provider and the payer.

That is one reason health insurance premiums can feel so confusing. The premium is not based only on how much care employees use. It is also affected by what the health plan has agreed to pay doctors, hospitals, clinics, labs, and other providers for that care.

This is where provider networks matter. A network is not just a list of doctors. It is also a set of payment relationships. A broad PPO network, a lower-cost HMO, Medicare, and an out-of-network arrangement may all pay differently for the same basic service. That does not mean anyone is doing something wrong. It means healthcare pricing is negotiated, layered, and often hard for employers to see.

For small businesses, understanding this can make health plan decisions much more practical. It helps explain why one plan may cost more than another, why HMOs may lower premiums, why PPOs offer more flexibility, and why network strategy belongs in every serious renewal review.
Medicare and Commercial Insurance Are Different Pricing Worlds

A good place to start is Medicare. Medicare is a government program with formal payment systems. It does not usually negotiate prices with every hospital and doctor in the same way a commercial insurance carrier does.

For many physician services, Medicare uses the Physician Fee Schedule. CMS explains that Medicare Physician Fee Schedule payments are based on relative value units, a conversion factor, and geographic adjustments. In simpler terms, Medicare uses a formula to decide what it will pay for many doctor and professional services.

For many inpatient hospital stays, Medicare uses the Inpatient Prospective Payment System, or IPPS. CMS explains that Medicare generally pays acute care hospitals a predetermined amount for each discharge, based on the average resources needed to treat similar cases, rather than paying separately for every individual item or service during the hospital stay.

That does not mean Medicare is simple. It is not. But the key point for a business owner is this: Medicare often pays through published formulas. Commercial insurance prices are usually based on negotiated contracts. That is a major difference. A hospital may receive one payment amount from Medicare, a different amount from one commercial PPO network, another amount from a different carrier’s HMO, and a very different amount from an out-of-network claim.
Commercial Insurance Often Pays More Than Medicare

Commercial employer health plans often pay providers more than Medicare does. RAND’s 2024 Hospital Price Transparency Study found that employers and private insurers paid hospitals an average of 254% of what Medicare would have paid for the same inpatient and outpatient services in 2022, with wide variation by state and hospital. That number is important, but it should be handled carefully. It does not prove that every hospital is overcharging. It does not prove that every insurer is failing to negotiate. It does not prove that Medicare always pays the “right” amount.

It simply shows that employer-sponsored commercial insurance operates in a different pricing environment than Medicare. For small business owners, the practical takeaway is simple: Your premium is affected not only by how often employees use healthcare, but also by what your plan pays when they do.
That is why network choice matters.
How Doctors May Be Paid

Doctors and other medical professionals can be paid in several ways. In many arrangements, doctors are paid fee-for-service. That means the doctor bills for a specific service, and the payer allows a contracted amount for that service. The payer may be Medicare, a commercial insurer, or another plan.

For example, if a doctor performs an office visit, the payment may be based on a fee schedule. Under Medicare, that fee schedule is formula-based. Under a commercial insurance contract, the allowed amount may be negotiated between the insurer and the provider group.

In some arrangements, doctors or medical groups may be paid through capitation. CMS defines capitation as a way of paying providers or organizations a predictable, upfront, set amount to cover the expected cost of all or some healthcare services for a patient over a period of time.
In plain English, fee-for-service pays when services happen. Capitation pays a set amount per patient over time.

Neither model is automatically good or bad. They create different incentives. Fee-for-service can reward volume because payment is tied to services provided. Capitation can reward prevention and cost control because the provider group receives a set amount and is responsible for managing care within that budget. But capitation also needs proper oversight, because a poorly designed system could create concerns about access or underuse of care.
This is why payment design matters. It shapes behavior.
How Hospitals May Be Paid
Hospitals can also be paid in different ways depending on the payer and contract.

Under Medicare’s inpatient hospital system, the payment is often tied to the type of case rather than every individual supply or service used during the hospital stay. CMS describes the IPPS as paying predetermined rates for each hospital discharge, with payment based on average national resource use for similar cases. Physicians are generally paid separately under the Physician Fee Schedule for their professional services during the inpatient stay.
Commercial insurance contracts can work differently.

A commercial insurer might pay a hospital based on negotiated rates for specific services. It might use case rates, per-diem rates, percentages of billed charges, outpatient fee schedules, or arrangements tied to Medicare rates. The exact contract terms are usually not visible to small employers.

That is part of the problem. The employer sees the premium. The employee sees the deductible or copay. But the underlying payment agreement between the insurance company and the hospital may be hidden from both.
That hidden pricing can affect claims. Claims affect premiums. So the contract still matters, even if the employer never sees it directly.
How a PPO Network Works

A PPO, or Preferred Provider Organization, usually gives employees more flexibility. Healthcare.gov explains that a PPO contracts with medical providers to create a network, and members pay less when they use providers in that network while still having the option to use out-of-network providers at an additional cost.
From the employee’s perspective, the advantage is choice. From the employer’s perspective, the tradeoff is cost.

A broad PPO may include many hospitals, doctor groups, and specialists. It may also offer out-of-network benefits. That can make employees more comfortable, especially if they are spread across multiple locations or have established doctors.

But that flexibility may mean the carrier has to include expensive providers in the network. If an important hospital system has strong negotiating power, the insurer may accept higher contracted rates to keep that provider in the network.
That is not sinister. It is negotiation.

The insurer wants a network employees will use. The hospital wants to be paid fairly, or as favorably as the market allows. The employer wants a premium that is affordable. The employee wants access. The final premium reflects that tug-of-war.
How an HMO Network Works
An HMO, or Health Maintenance Organization, usually has a more limited network than a broad PPO.

Healthcare.gov explains that an HMO usually limits coverage to care from doctors who work for or contract with the HMO, and generally will not cover out-of-network care except in emergencies. HMOs may also require members to live or work in the service area and often focus on integrated care, prevention, and wellness.
That structure can help lower costs in several ways.
First, the HMO may contract with a smaller group of providers. That gives the plan more ability to steer members toward certain doctors, clinics, hospitals, or medical groups.

Second, some HMO arrangements use more coordinated care. Employees may select or be assigned to a primary care doctor. Referrals may be required for some specialists. The plan may try to avoid unnecessary high-cost care by managing where and how care is delivered.

Third, some HMO or integrated-care arrangements may use payment models such as capitation. Instead of paying only when services happen, the plan may pay a provider group a set amount per member per month to manage some or all of that member’s care. CMS describes capitation as a set payment made upfront to cover expected healthcare services for a patient over a period of time.

This changes the financial incentives. A PPO often gives more freedom and pays through negotiated claims as services are used. An HMO may use a more controlled network and, in some arrangements, more predictable provider payment. That is one reason HMOs can sometimes produce lower premiums.

But there is a tradeoff. Employees may have less flexibility. Out-of-network care may not be covered except in emergencies. Some employees may dislike referrals or network limits. That is why an HMO should be evaluated based on actual provider fit, not just price.
A Simple Example: One Procedure, Different Payment Paths
Let’s use a simplified example.
Assume an employee needs an outpatient procedure. The hospital’s public “sticker price” is $12,000.

That sticker price is not necessarily what anyone actually pays. Here is how payment might look under different arrangements. These numbers are only examples. Actual prices depend on the contract, service, location, provider, and plan.
This example shows why “the price” of healthcare is not one simple number. The payment depends on the payer, the network, the contract, and the plan design.
Who Gets Paid in a Typical Claim?
A small business owner does not need to know every billing detail, but it helps to understand the basic flow.

The employer pays premium to the insurance carrier. Employees may also pay part of the premium through payroll deductions. When an employee receives care, the provider bills the insurance plan. The plan applies the contract, determines the allowed amount, subtracts the employee’s deductible, copay, or coinsurance, and pays the provider according to the plan rules.

The provider may receive money from both the insurer and the employee. The insurer keeps part of the premium for administration, claims processing, network contracting, reserves, taxes, and margin. The employer does not usually see the detailed contract rates behind each claim in a fully insured plan.

In a level-funded or self-funded arrangement, the employer may see more claims and cost data, depending on size, privacy rules, vendor reporting, and plan structure. But even then, the provider contracts are usually still controlled by the carrier, network, or third-party administrator.
The key point is this: The health plan is not just paying medical bills. It is applying a network contract. That is why the network matters.
Why Broad Networks May Cost More

Broad networks are popular because they reduce disruption. Employees can keep more doctors. They may have more hospital choices. They may have out-of-network options. This matters when a company has employees in multiple cities, employees with dependents, or employees who value provider flexibility.

But broad networks can also make it harder for the insurer to exclude high-cost providers. If employees expect access to certain hospital systems, the insurer may need those systems in the network to make the plan attractive. That can give major provider systems negotiating leverage.

Again, this is not about blame. It is normal market behavior. The provider wants strong payment. The insurer wants a usable network. The employer wants affordable premiums. The employee wants access. Broad networks often try to satisfy more of those demands at once, and that can raise cost.
Why Focused Networks and HMOs May Cost Less

A focused network or HMO may lower cost by being more selective. The plan may contract with a narrower group of hospitals, physician groups, and clinics. It may guide members toward lower-cost facilities or more coordinated care. It may reduce out-of-network exposure. It may use primary care more deliberately.

That can lower the plan’s expected claims. But lower cost only matters if the network still works for employees. If the HMO includes the doctors and hospitals employees already use, it may be a strong option. If it excludes important providers, employees may see it as a major downgrade.
That is why a doctor match review can be so useful for small employers. Before rejecting an HMO, the employer can check whether employees’ important providers are actually in the HMO network.
Sometimes the lower-cost network is more workable than people assume.
Why This Matters to Small Employers
Small employers usually cannot change how hospitals and insurance companies negotiate. But they can make better plan decisions when they understand the system.
A business owner reviewing a renewal should ask more than: “What is the premium?”

Better questions include: What network are we buying? Are employees using high-cost providers? Does a lower-cost HMO include the doctors employees care about? Are we paying extra for broad access that employees may not need? Could we offer a lower-cost base plan and a PPO buy-up option?

Those questions do not attack doctors, hospitals, or insurers. They simply recognize that networks are part of the pricing system. For a small business, that can turn a confusing renewal into a more thoughtful strategy discussion.
What This Does Not Mean
This article is not saying that doctors are paid too much, hospitals are bad, or insurers are hiding everything.

Healthcare pricing is complicated. Providers have real costs. Hospitals operate emergency departments, maintain expensive equipment, employ specialized staff and treat patients with different needs. Insurers build networks, process claims, manage contracts, and take financial risk.
The problem for employers is not that one side is always wrong. The problem is that the employer often sees only the premium, not the payment system behind it.
Understanding that system helps small businesses ask better questions.
The Bottom Line
The same healthcare service can be paid very differently depending on whether the payer is Medicare, a PPO network, an HMO network, or an out-of-network arrangement.

Medicare often pays using published formulas. Commercial insurers negotiate rates with doctors, hospitals, and provider systems. PPOs usually offer broader access and more flexibility. HMOs often use a more focused network and may rely more heavily on coordinated care or alternative provider payment models.
For small businesses, the practical lesson is simple: Provider networks are not just about which doctors employees can use. They are also about what the health plan pays for care.
That is why network choice can affect premiums, and why a strong renewal review should look behind the rate to understand the network, payment structure, and employee access tradeoffs.
FAQ SECTION
1. Why can the same healthcare service cost different amounts?

The payment can vary depending on whether the payer is Medicare, a commercial PPO, an HMO, or an out-of-network arrangement. Each may use different payment rules, negotiated rates, or provider contracts.
2. How does Medicare pay doctors?
For many physician and professional services, Medicare uses the Physician Fee Schedule. CMS says these payments are based on relative value units, a conversion factor, and geographic adjustments.
3. How does Medicare pay hospitals?

For many inpatient hospital stays, Medicare uses the Inpatient Prospective Payment System, which pays predetermined amounts based on similar cases rather than paying separately for each item used during the stay.
4. Why do commercial insurance plans often pay more than Medicare?

Commercial rates are usually negotiated between insurers and providers. RAND’s 2024 study found that employers and private insurers paid hospitals an average of 254% of what Medicare would have paid for the same inpatient and outpatient services in 2022.
5. How does a PPO network affect provider payment?

A PPO usually pays in-network providers based on negotiated allowed amounts. Employees may also use out-of-network providers, usually at higher cost. Healthcare.gov describes PPOs as networks where members pay less for in-network providers but can use out-of-network providers for an additional cost.
6. How does an HMO network affect provider payment?

An HMO usually limits coverage to providers that work for or contract with the HMO, except in emergencies. Some HMO or managed-care arrangements may use more coordinated care or payment models such as capitation.
7. Does a lower-cost HMO always mean worse access?
No. A lower-cost HMO may work well if it includes the doctors, hospitals, and specialists employees already use. If important providers are missing, the savings may not be worth the disruption.
8. What should small employers ask when comparing networks?

Small employers should ask which providers are included, how the network affects premium, whether key employee doctors are in network, and whether a lower-cost base plan plus a broader PPO buy-up option would make sense.

Health insurance premiums are easier to evaluate when you understand the network behind the plan.

title: How Reviewing Doctors Can Lower Your Health Insurance Cost
description: Many small business owners assume employees will reject an HMO or smaller provider network. Sometimes they will but, sometimes they will not.

blocks.text: Many small business owners assume employees will reject an HMO or smaller provider network. Sometimes they will but, sometimes they will not.

Employees usually do not care about having the biggest network in theory. They care about something more personal: whether their doctors, hospitals, pediatricians, specialists, therapists, and local medical groups are included. That creates a practical opportunity for small employers.

Before rejecting a lower-cost HMO or focused-network plan, a small business can do a simple doctor match review. The goal is to compare the providers employees actually care about against the network in the lower-cost plan. This is one of the few areas where being small can be an advantage. A company with 20 employees may be able to review provider fit in a way a company with 2,000 employees usually cannot. Large employers often need broad assumptions. Small employers can sometimes be more precise.

The point is not to ask employees private medical questions. The employer does not need to know anyone’s diagnosis, prescription, treatment history, or medical condition. The review should focus only on provider names and locations. Done correctly, a doctor match review can help answer a useful renewal question: Could we move to a lower-cost network without creating major provider disruption?
What Is a Doctor Match Review?

A doctor match review is a simple comparison between two lists. The first list is the providers employees want to keep using. The second list is the providers included in the lower-cost health plan network.

For example, a company may currently offer a broad PPO plan. At renewal, the employer receives a quote for a lower-cost HMO. Instead of assuming the HMO will not work, the employer asks: “Are the doctors employees already use included in this network?”
If the answer is mostly yes, the lower-cost plan may be more realistic than expected. If the answer is mostly no, the employer may decide the savings are not worth the disruption.

This is not a perfect process. Provider directories can be wrong or outdated. CMS notes that provider directories are not always accurate and recommends contacting the insurance company when network status is unclear. But even with that limitation, a doctor match review is better than guessing.
Why This Can Affect Health Insurance Costs

Provider networks are not just access tools. They can affect plan pricing. CMS rate-review instructions allow plan-level adjustments for a plan’s provider network, delivery system characteristics, and utilization management practices. In plain English, the network can affect what the carrier expects to pay for care.
That is why a broad PPO may cost more than a more focused HMO or EPO. The broader plan may include more providers, more hospital systems, and more flexibility.

That flexibility can be valuable. KFF’s 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey found that PPOs remain the most common employer plan type, covering 46% of covered workers. KFF also describes narrow networks as plans that limit participating providers to reduce costs, with 9% of firms offering health benefits offering a narrow network plan in 2025. This begs the question: Are we paying extra for provider access our employees actually need?
Why Small Employers Have an Advantage

Large employers have more data and more resources. But small employers often know their workforce better. A 15-person company may know that most employees live in the same few ZIP codes. A 25-person firm may know that several employees use the same local hospital system. A 40-person contractor may know that affordability matters more to employees than broad national access. That practical knowledge matters.
A large employer usually cannot manually check every employee’s doctors before changing plans. A small employer often can do a lighter, more personal review which could save everyone a lot of money
How to Ask Employees Without Asking Medical Questions

The review should be simple and respectful. The employer should not ask why someone sees a doctor. It should not ask about conditions, medications, procedures, or diagnoses. The way to ask is: “If we review lower-cost health plan options, are there any doctors, hospitals, specialists, pediatricians, therapists, or medical groups that are important for you or your family to keep in network?”

Employees can provide provider names and locations. The location matters because a doctor may participate at one office but not another. The exact plan name also matters because a provider may accept one carrier network but not another. The employer or advisor can then compare those providers against the lower-cost network being considered. You could also simply provide the network link to the employees and ask them to verify their preferred providers. This keeps the process focused on access, not private health information.
Why the Results Matter

The results of a doctor match review can change the renewal conversation. If most important providers are already included in the lower-cost network, the employer may be able to offer that plan with more confidence. If many important providers are missing, the employer may decide the savings are not worth the frustration.
The review can also support a two-option strategy.

For example, the employer might offer a lower-cost HMO as the base plan and make it very affordable through a stronger company contribution. Employees who want broader access could still choose a PPO buy-up option and pay more for that added flexibility.

That approach does not force everyone into the smaller network. It gives employees a choice while helping the company manage cost. For some small businesses, that is a better strategy than choosing one plan and hoping it works for everyone.
A Simple Example

Imagine a 22-person technology company in Austin currently offers a broad PPO plan. The renewal increase is uncomfortable, and the employer is considering a lower-cost HMO. The owner worries employees will see the HMO as a downgrade.
Before deciding, the company asks employees to voluntarily list any providers they want to keep in network. The company does not ask why those providers matter.
After checking the HMO network, the advisor finds that most key providers are already included. A few are not. Now the owner has better information.

The company may offer the HMO as the low-cost base plan and keep the PPO as a buy-up option. Employees whose doctors are in the HMO can save money. Employees who want the broader network can pay more for it.
When This Strategy May Not Work

A doctor match review is useful, but it is not magic. It may not work well if employees are spread across many states, if the workforce has many dependents in different locations, or if provider access is already a sensitive issue. Some employees may also be uncomfortable sharing provider names, even without medical details.

Directories can also be imperfect. CMS has warned that provider directories are not always accurate, and prior CMS reviews of Medicare Advantage directories found significant inaccuracies. So the review should not be treated as a guarantee. It is a practical screening tool. The goal is to reduce avoidable disruption, not to promise that every provider relationship will stay unchanged forever.
The Bottom Line

A doctor match review is a simple way for small businesses to make better health insurance decisions. Instead of assuming a lower-cost HMO or focused network will not work, the employer can check whether employees’ important providers are already included. If the match is strong, the business may be able to move toward a lower-cost option with more confidence. If the match is weak, the employer can avoid a change that may create unnecessary frustration.

This is one area where small employers may have an advantage. They are often small enough to review provider fit in a practical, personal way. For small businesses, that can be the difference between simply accepting a higher premium and building a more thoughtful health insurance strategy.
FAQ SECTION
1. What is a doctor match review?
A doctor match review compares the doctors, hospitals, specialists, and other providers employees want to keep using against the provider network of a health plan being considered.
2. Can a doctor match review help lower health insurance costs?
It may. If many employees’ current providers are already included in a lower-cost HMO or focused network, the employer may be able to offer that plan without creating major disruption.
3. Should employers ask employees for medical information?
No. Employers should avoid asking about diagnoses, prescriptions, conditions, or treatment history. The review should focus only on provider names and locations.
4. Why do provider networks affect premiums?

Provider networks can affect what a carrier expects to pay for care. CMS rate-review instructions identify provider network and delivery system characteristics as plan-level factors in rate development.
5. Are provider directories always accurate?
No. CMS says provider directories are not always accurate and recommends contacting the insurance company when network status is unclear.
6. Can a small business offer both an HMO and a PPO?

In some fully insured small-group arrangements, an employer may be able to offer a lower-cost HMO or focused-network plan along with a broader PPO buy-up option. Carrier rules, contribution requirements, participation rules, and plan availability need to be reviewed.
7. Is a lower-cost network always the right choice?
No. A lower-cost network only works if it gives employees reasonable access to the providers they need. The savings must be weighed against possible disruption.
Thinking About Moving to a Lower-Cost Network?
Before assuming employees will reject an HMO or focused-network plan, it may be worth checking whether their important providers are already included.

blocks.text: When small business owners compare health insurance plans, they usually start with the obvious numbers: the monthly premium, the deductible, the copays, and the out-of-pocket maximum. That is understandable. Those numbers are easy to see.
But one of the most important cost drivers is not always as obvious. It is the provider network.

A provider network is the group of doctors, hospitals, clinics, specialists, labs, and other healthcare providers that have contracts with the insurance carrier. When employees stay in network, they usually pay less. When they go out of network, they may pay more, or they may have limited coverage except in emergencies.
Most employees think about the network in simple terms: “Can I keep my doctor?” or “Is my hospital covered?” Business owners need to look at it one step deeper.

The network does not just affect access. It also affects cost. CMS rate-review instructions specifically identify a plan’s provider network, delivery system characteristics, and utilization management practices as factors that may affect plan-level pricing. In plain English, the network can influence what the insurance company expects to pay for healthcare.
That means two plans can look similar on the surface but still have very different pricing because the underlying networks are different.

For small businesses, this is an important part of the renewal conversation. A broader network may give employees more freedom. A smaller or more focused network may help reduce premiums. The best choice depends on the company, the employees, and the employer’s overall benefits strategy.
A Network Is Not Just a List of Doctors

It is easy to think of a provider network as a directory. From the employee’s perspective, that is how it often feels. They want to know if their primary care doctor is covered, whether their child’s pediatrician is in network, and whether they can still use the hospital system they know.
Those questions matter. If employees cannot use the plan easily, they may not value it, even if the premium is lower.

But from the insurance company’s perspective, the network is also a pricing tool. The carrier looks at which hospitals, doctors, and facilities are included in the network. It also looks at the prices it has negotiated with those providers. A plan that includes more expensive hospital systems may have higher expected claims. A plan that steers care toward lower-cost providers may have lower expected claims. That does not mean the lower-cost network is always better. It means the network is one of the reasons one plan may cost more than another.
This is why a small business should not compare health plans only by premium and deductible. The network may be doing a lot of work behind the scenes.
Why Broad Networks Often Cost More

A broad network usually gives employees more choice. It may include more hospital systems, more physician groups, more specialists, and more out-of-network flexibility. For employees, that can feel safer and more convenient.

For example, a small engineering firm in the Chicago suburbs may have employees spread across several counties. A broad PPO network can make it easier for employees to keep their doctors and avoid disruption. A Texas technology company with employees in Austin, Dallas, Houston, and San Antonio may also value a broad network because employees are not all using the same local medical system.

That flexibility can be worth paying for but, broader access often comes with a higher price. If a network includes expensive hospitals and high-cost provider systems, the insurance carrier expects higher claims. Those expected claims can show up in the premium.

PPOs remain the most common employer health plan type. KFF’s 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey found that 46% of covered workers were enrolled in PPOs. KFF also explains that PPOs allow both in-network and out-of-network care, usually with lower cost-sharing when employees stay in network.
That flexibility is part of why employees often like PPOs. It is also one reason employers need to ask whether the extra access is worth the extra cost.
Why Narrow or Focused Networks Can Lower Premiums
A narrow network limits the number of participating providers.

At first, that may sound like a bad thing. Sometimes it is. If the network does not include the doctors and hospitals employees need, the plan can create frustration quickly. But a focused network can also be a legitimate cost-control tool.

The basic idea is simple: instead of giving employees access to almost every provider, the plan directs employees toward a smaller group of providers that may have better pricing, better coordination, or more predictable costs.

KFF describes narrow network plans as plans that restrict the number of participating providers in order to reduce costs. In 2025, 9% of firms offering health benefits offered a narrow network plan. A narrower network may work well when employees live in the same general area and the network includes the providers they already use. It may also work when the premium savings are meaningful enough to make coverage more affordable for both the business and employees.

But this is where small businesses need to be careful. A narrow network that saves money but causes employees to lose important doctors may not be a good tradeoff. A lower premium can still be a bad value if the plan becomes harder to use.
The Price of Healthcare Can Vary Widely
Provider networks matter because healthcare prices are not the same everywhere.

The same general service can cost very different amounts depending on the hospital, facility, or provider group. RAND’s employer price transparency study found that in 2022, employers and private insurers paid hospitals an average of 254% of what Medicare would have paid for the same inpatient and outpatient services at the same facilities.

That is a big gap, and it helps explain why networks matter. If a plan includes high-cost providers and employees often use them, the cost of claims can be higher. If a plan has stronger contracts with lower-cost providers, expected claims may be lower. This does not mean one hospital is automatically better or worse than another. It means the price of healthcare is not uniform.

Small business owners understand this in almost every other area of business. Two law firms may charge different rates. Two software vendors may offer different pricing. Two contractors may quote different amounts for the same job.
Healthcare works the same way, except the prices are much harder to see.
PPO, HMO, EPO, and POS: What Employers Should Understand
The labels can get confusing, but the basic idea is manageable.

A PPO usually gives employees more flexibility. They can use in-network providers at a lower cost and may have some coverage for out-of-network providers. This is one reason PPOs are popular, but that flexibility often comes with higher premiums.

An HMO is usually more controlled. Employees generally need to use the plan’s network, and out-of-network care is often not covered except in emergencies. That can help control costs, but employees may feel restricted if they are used to broader access. KFF defines HMOs as plans that do not cover non-emergency services provided out of network.

An EPO is also network-focused. Employees generally need to stay in network, except for emergencies. It may not always feel as managed as an HMO, but employees still need to be careful about which providers are included.
A POS plan is more of a hybrid. It may include features of both HMO and PPO designs.

The key point is this: the label does not tell the whole story. One PPO may have a better local network than another PPO. One HMO may be perfectly workable if the network includes the doctors and hospitals employees already use.
The right question is not simply, “Is this a PPO or an HMO?” The better question is: Does this network fit our employees well enough to justify the cost?
The Employee Disruption Problem
Network changes can look great in a spreadsheet and still cause problems in real life.

This is especially true for small businesses. In a 15-person or 25-person company, a few unhappy employees can create a lot of friction. If someone loses access to a child’s specialist, a trusted therapist, an OB/GYN, or a hospital system they rely on, the issue becomes personal very quickly. That does not mean employers should avoid every network change. It means they should review the tradeoff before making a decision.

A business owner should think about where employees actually live, not just where the business is located. A company based in one part of Chicago may have employees commuting from several suburbs. A Texas employer may have workers spread across multiple metro areas. A plan that looks strong near the office may not work as well near employees’ homes.
This is one reason employee ZIP codes matter during a plan review. The network needs to work where people actually seek care.
Mental Health Access Should Not Be an Afterthought
Many employers review hospitals and primary care doctors first. That makes sense, but mental health access deserves special attention.

KFF’s 2025 survey found that employers were more confident about timely access to primary care and specialty care than mental health care. Among firms offering health benefits, 92% believed their largest plan had enough providers for timely primary care access, and 89% believed it had enough for specialty care. Only 70% believed it had enough mental health providers for timely access. That gap matters.

A network may look fine on paper but still be weak for behavioral health. For employees dealing with stress, anxiety, depression, family issues, or substance-use concerns, “covered” does not always mean “easy to access.” For small employers that care about retention, productivity, and employee well-being, mental health access is not just a nice extra. It can be an important part of plan quality.
The Two-Option Strategy: A Practical Way to Use Networks
A small business does not always have to choose one network for everyone.

In some fully insured small-group arrangements, an employer may be able to offer more than one plan option. That can create a useful cost-containment strategy without forcing every employee into the same tradeoff. For example, a company might offer a lower-cost HMO or focused-network plan as the main option. The employer could make that plan very affordable by contributing more heavily toward it.

At the same time, the company might also offer a broader PPO plan for employees who want more provider choice. Those employees would still have access to the broader network, but they would pay more of the added cost themselves. This can be a smart middle ground.
The company is not saying, “Everyone has to take the smaller network.” It is saying: “We will make the cost-effective plan very affordable. If you want broader access, you can buy up.”

That approach can help the company manage its budget while still respecting employee choice. This strategy works best when the lower-cost plan is genuinely usable. If the HMO or focused network includes the providers employees already use, the plan may be attractive. If it is too restrictive, employees may see it as a downgrade.

Carrier rules, contribution requirements, participation rules, and plan availability also matter. This is not something to set up casually. But when it is available and communicated clearly, it can be a better solution than choosing one plan and hoping it works for everyone.
A Simple Doctor Match Review Can Reduce Guesswork

Before assuming employees will reject a lower-cost HMO or focused network, a small employer can do a simple doctor match review. The idea is straightforward: ask employees whether there are any doctors, hospitals, pediatricians, specialists, or mental health providers that are especially important for them or their families to keep in network. The employer does not need to ask about medical conditions, prescriptions, diagnoses, or treatment history. The review should focus only on provider names and locations.

This can be a real advantage for small businesses. A large employer with hundreds or thousands of employees usually cannot check every employee’s preferred providers before changing plans. A small employer with 5 to 50 employees may be able to do a more practical review. If many of the important providers already participate in the lower-cost HMO or focused network, the employer may be able to offer that plan with more confidence. If many important providers are missing, the employer may decide the savings are not worth the disruption.

This is a good example of why network strategy should not be based on assumptions. Sometimes a lower-cost network is more workable than employees expect. Other times, the provider disruption is too significant. The point is to check before making the decision.
How Networks Fit With Fully Insured and Level-Funded Plans

Provider networks matter in both fully insured and level-funded plans. In a fully insured plan, the carrier bundles the network, claims risk, administration, and premium into one product. The employer chooses from the options available in that market.

In a level-funded plan, the employer may see more of the cost structure, including expected claims funding, administrative costs, and stop-loss protection. But the network still matters because it influences what claims may cost. A level-funded plan with a poor network fit can create employee frustration. A fully insured plan with an expensive broad network can create unnecessary cost. The funding method matters, but it does not replace the need to review the network carefully.
This is why a good renewal review should look at more than the premium. It should also ask whether the network, plan design, funding structure, and employer contribution strategy fit together.
When a Smaller Network May Make Sense

A smaller or more focused network may make sense when the employees are mostly local, the network includes the providers they already use, and the premium savings are meaningful. This can be especially useful for a small business trying to keep employee contributions affordable. If the lower-cost network is strong in the area, employees may prefer a plan that costs them less each paycheck, even if it gives them fewer provider choices.

But the employer should not assume employees will accept the tradeoff automatically. A network change should be explained clearly. Employees should understand what is changing, which providers are included, and what they need to do before scheduling care.
The goal is not just to reduce premium. The goal is to reduce cost without making the plan feel unusable.
When a Broad Network May Be Worth Paying For

A broader network may be worth the cost when employees are spread across multiple cities or states, when they have established specialist relationships, or when the employer is trying to compete for talent against larger companies.

Some employers also choose broader networks simply to reduce disruption. That can be a reasonable decision. If the premium difference is manageable and employees highly value choice, a broad PPO-style network may be worth paying for.
The mistake is not choosing a broad network. The mistake is choosing it automatically without asking whether the company is paying for access employees actually need.
A Better Way to Review the Network
A practical network review should start with real employee needs.

Are the major local hospitals included? Are common physician groups included? Does the plan work near employee home ZIP codes? Are mental health providers available? Are employees likely to lose doctors? Is there out-of-network coverage? Are there referral rules? Could the employer offer both a lower-cost option and a broader buy-up option?
Those questions are more useful than simply asking which plan has the lowest premium. A good plan review should help the business owner understand the tradeoff:
How much are we saving, and what access are employees giving up?
Sometimes the savings are worth it. Sometimes they are not. The value comes from making that decision intentionally.
The Bottom Line

Provider networks are one of the most important hidden drivers of small business health insurance premiums. A broader network may give employees more flexibility, but it can also increase expected claims costs. A narrower or tiered network may reduce premiums, but it can create access issues if the fit is poor.

For small businesses in Illinois and Texas, the best answer is not automatically “broad network” or “narrow network.” The best answer depends on where employees live, which providers they use, how much disruption they can tolerate, and how the company wants to structure its contribution.

In some cases, the smartest strategy may be to offer both: a lower-cost network plan with a stronger employer contribution, and a broader network option for employees who want more choice and are willing to pay more. A smart health plan review should always ask: Are we paying for the right network — or just the familiar one?
FAQ SECTION
1. How do provider networks affect health insurance premiums?

Provider networks affect premiums because they influence what the health plan expects to pay for care. CMS rate-review instructions identify provider network, delivery system characteristics, and utilization management practices as factors that may affect plan-level pricing.
2. Are PPO plans usually more expensive than HMO or EPO plans?

PPO plans often cost more because they usually offer broader access and out-of-network flexibility. PPOs are also the most common employer plan type, with 46% of covered workers enrolled in PPOs in KFF’s 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey.
3. What is a narrow network health plan?
A narrow network plan limits the number of participating providers, usually to help reduce costs. KFF reported that 9% of firms offering health benefits offered a narrow network plan in 2025.
4. Is a narrow network always bad for employees?

No. A narrow network can work well if it includes the doctors, hospitals, and specialists employees actually use. It becomes a problem when employees lose access to important providers or have trouble finding care.
5. Can a small business offer both an HMO and a PPO?

In some fully insured small-group arrangements, an employer may be able to offer more than one plan option, such as a lower-cost HMO and a broader PPO. Carrier rules, contribution requirements, participation requirements, and plan availability should be reviewed before setting this up.
6. Why does mental health access matter in a provider network?

A plan can have strong hospital and primary care access but still have limited behavioral health access. KFF’s 2025 survey found employers were less confident about timely mental health access than primary or specialty care access.
7. Should small businesses always choose the cheapest network?
No. The cheapest plan may create employee disruption if the network is too restrictive. Employers should compare premium savings against provider access, employee expectations, and disruption risk.
Not Sure Whether Your Health Plan Network Is Helping or Hurting?
A lower premium is not always a better deal, and a broader network is not always worth the extra cost.

title: If Your Health Plan Has Low Claims, Who Gets the Savings?
description: Imagine a small business has a surprisingly good health insurance year. Employees use the plan, but there are no major surgeries, no catastrophic hospital claims, and no unusually expensive ongoing treatments. The owner ...

blocks.text: Imagine a small business has a surprisingly good health insurance year. Employees use the plan, but there are no major surgeries, no catastrophic hospital claims, and no unusually expensive ongoing treatments. The owner knows the company paid a large amount in premiums and assumes that a better-than-expected claims year should count for something.
Then the renewal arrives and the premium still goes up.

That experience frustrates many small business owners, especially those with younger or relatively healthy workforces. They naturally wonder: "If our claims were lower than expected, who benefited from that"?
The answer depends heavily on how the health plan is funded.

In a traditional fully insured small-group health plan, the employer generally does not receive a refund simply because its own employees had a low-claims year. Any Medical Loss Ratio rebate is based on the insurance carrier’s results across a broader state and market segment, not on one employer’s specific claims experience.

In some level-funded health plans, the employer may have an opportunity to receive a surplus refund if claims come in below the amount funded for claims, subject to the carrier’s contract terms and applicable rules.
That difference gets to the heart of a bigger question: Does your health plan structure allow your business to benefit when claims run well or, does that upside stay somewhere else?
First, What Is the 80/20 Rule?
The Affordable Care Act created a rule known as the Medical Loss Ratio, or MLR, requirement.

In the individual and small-group health insurance markets, carriers generally must spend at least 80% of premium revenue on medical care and activities that improve healthcare quality. If they fall below that threshold, they may owe rebates.

This is often called the 80/20 rule. Simply put, most of the premium dollars should go toward healthcare and a smaller share can go toward running the insurance company. That sounds like a clear protection for consumers. And in some ways, it is. But the rule may not be working quite the way many people assumed it would.
The 80/20 Rule May Not Reward Lower Costs the Way People Expect

The rule is based on a percentage of premiums, not on a fixed dollar limit. So if the total cost of healthcare rises, premiums usually rise too. And when premiums rise, the dollar amount left over for administration, business expenses, and profit also rises all while the insurer still follows the 80/20 rule.
Here is a simple example:

In both cases, the insurer meets the 80/20 rule. But when the total premium goes up, the available non-claims dollars go up too. That does not mean insurance companies are purposely trying to make healthcare more expensive. That would be too strong a claim. But it does mean the rule may not create as much pressure to lower healthcare costs as many people assumed. If an insurer finds ways to reduce claims significantly, that may reduce the total premium base it can work from. And if too little of the premium dollar is spent on healthcare, the carrier may owe rebates.

Economists have raised this concern directly. A peer-reviewed study found that insurers affected by the Medical Loss Ratio rule increased claims spending after the rule took effect by about 7% in the individual market and 2% in the group market. The authors said the findings were consistent with a system that limits profit margins, but not necessarily total profit dollars.
In plain English: The rule was designed to stop insurers from keeping too much of each premium dollar. But it may not strongly reward the whole system for making healthcare less expensive overall.
Meanwhile, Healthcare Costs Keep Rising
The 80/20 rule was created to make health insurance spending more consumer-friendly. But it did not stop healthcare costs from continuing to climb.
When the ACA was signed in 2010, total U.S. healthcare spending was about $2.6 trillion, or $8,402 per person. By 2024, national health spending had reached $5.3 trillion, or $15,474 per person.
Employer health insurance premiums rose sharply too. In 2010, the average annual premium for employer-sponsored family coverage was $13,770. By 2025, it had reached $26,993.
Those numbers do not prove that the 80/20 rule caused healthcare costs to rise. Many other forces have driven costs upward, including:
Hospital prices
Prescription drug costs
New treatments and technologies
Provider consolidation
Increased use of medical services
Chronic disease and high-cost conditions

But the numbers do help explain why a small business owner might fairly ask: "If the system was redesigned to protect premium dollars, why do premiums still keep rising and, who actually benefits when costs come in lower than expected?"
The 80/20 Rule Is Not the Same as a Refund for Your Business
This is the part many employers do not realize.

If a fully insured carrier owes a rebate under the Medical Loss Ratio rule, the calculation is based on aggregated results across a state and market segment. It is not calculated based on whether your specific business had low claims. Federal rulemaking materials state clearly that rebates are not based on a particular group health plan’s experience or a particular subscriber’s experience.
In plain English:
Your company can have an excellent claims year and receive no rebate.
Another company can have a terrible claims year and still be part of a market segment where a rebate is issued.
The rebate calculation is about the insurer’s broader results, not about whether your own business “beat expectations.”

This is a critical distinction for small business owners. A low-claims year in a fully insured small-group plan does not usually create a direct financial upside for that employer. The carrier has absorbed the risk of high claims, but it also generally retains the benefit of lower claims within the broader insurance pool, subject to Medical Loss Ratio rules.
Why This Can Feel Misaligned for Some Small Businesses

Fully insured health insurance provides valuable certainty. The employer pays a fixed premium. If claims explode, the carrier bears that risk. That protection has real value. But the tradeoff is important: The employer pays for predictability, and in exchange, generally gives up the direct upside of a low-claims year.

For many small businesses, that tradeoff is perfectly acceptable. A company with volatile claims risk, an older workforce, or limited appetite for plan complexity may value the simplicity of fully insured coverage. But some employers look at that tradeoff differently.
A younger, relatively healthy business may think:
“We are paying into a large premium pool.”
“Our own claims are often lower than we expect.”
“If there is favorable experience, we rarely see that come back to us directly.”
“Is there a structure where we can share in that upside while still limiting downside risk?”
That question often leads to a discussion of level-funded health plans.
How Level-Funded Plans Change the Conversation
A level-funded health plan is generally designed to feel predictable from a budgeting standpoint while making more of the underlying cost structure visible.
The employer typically pays a fixed monthly amount that covers:
Expected claims funding
Administrative costs
Stop-loss protection against unusually high claims

If actual claims run lower than expected, some level-funded arrangements may offer a surplus refund at the end of the plan year, depending on the contract terms and applicable rules. That is a materially different employer experience.
In a fully insured model, when claims come in low, the employer usually does not receive a direct group-specific refund
In a level-funded model, when claims come in low, the employer may receive part of the favorable claims experience back through a contractual surplus refund

This does not mean level-funded plans are automatically better. They are not. Underwriting, eligibility, state availability, contract terms, stop-loss structure, claims volatility, and employer fit all matter.
But the “who benefits from a good claims year?” question is one of the clearest ways to explain why level funding can be compelling for the right small business.
Are Level-Funded Refunds the Same as “Getting the Insurer’s Profit”?
Not exactly.

A level-funded refund is not literally the employer taking back “insurance company profit.” It is better understood as the employer potentially receiving part of the unused claims funding if the plan’s actual claims come in below the amount set aside for claims, subject to the plan’s contract.
Still, from the employer’s perspective, the practical contrast is real:
In a fully insured plan, favorable claims experience generally benefits the broader insurance pool first.
In a level-funded plan, favorable claims experience may be shared more directly with the employer.
That is an important strategic distinction.
The Real Question Is Not “Are Insurers Bad?”
It is easy to turn this conversation into an attack on insurance companies. That is not the most useful path for a business owner.
The better question is: "Does my plan structure align the financial incentives the way I want them aligned?"

A fully insured carrier is paid to take the full claims risk and deliver a stable premium. In that model, the carrier needs to manage claims, comply with Medical Loss Ratio rules, and remain financially sound.

A level-funded arrangement still includes administrative fees and stop-loss protection, but it creates a more visible connection between the employer’s own claims experience and the employer’s potential financial outcome.
Neither approach is universally right. But owners should understand the difference.
Why This Matters for Small Businesses
Many small businesses are squeezed between two realities: They need a credible health plan to recruit and retain employees but they cannot afford to treat every renewal as a blank check.
For employers with favorable demographics or relatively stable health experience, it is reasonable to ask whether a fully insured structure is still the best fit.
This is especially true if the business owner feels:
“We keep paying more, but our own claims do not seem to explain it.”
“The fully insured model gives us no visible upside in good years.”
“We want to understand alternatives before accepting another renewal.”
That does not mean every small business should move to level funding. But it does mean the question is worth exploring.
A Good Claims Year Should Start a Better Conversation
If your company has low claims, the first step is not to demand a refund from a fully insured carrier. That is usually not how the product is designed.
The better step is to ask:
How does our current plan handle favorable claims experience?
Are we in a structure where our own group’s performance matters financially?
Would a level-funded comparison be appropriate?
Do we value maximum predictability more than potential upside?
Are we paying for a funding model that fits the company we have today?
Those questions lead to a much more useful benefits strategy discussion than simply chasing the lowest monthly premium.
The Bottom Line
The ACA’s 80/20 Medical Loss Ratio rule was designed to make sure insurers spend most premium dollars on healthcare and quality-improvement activities. It created an important consumer protection.

But it may not reward lower total healthcare costs as strongly as many people assume. Because it is based on a percentage of premium, rising healthcare costs can still leave more total dollars available for administration, expenses, and profit while the carrier remains within the rule. Economists have raised that concern directly, and healthcare spending and employer premiums have continued rising sharply since the ACA became law.
For small business owners, though, the most practical takeaway is simpler: In a fully insured plan, your business usually does not directly receive the financial benefit of its own good claims year.
Medical Loss Ratio rebates are based on broader carrier results by state and market, not on one employer’s specific experience.

That is one reason level-funded plans deserve consideration for some small businesses. They may offer a more direct way to participate in favorable claims experience through a potential surplus refund, while still including protection against large claims.
The right plan is not the same for every employer. But every owner should understand: Who benefits when claims come in lower than expected?
Wondering Whether Your Business Should Share in a Good Claims Year?

If your company is paying rising health insurance premiums while seeing relatively favorable employee claims experience, it may be worth reviewing whether your current funding structure still makes sense.
