title: What is Actually Inside Your Health Insurance Premium?
description: A small business owner receives a health insurance renewal and sees one number: The premium.

blocks.text: A small business owner receives a health insurance renewal and sees one number: The premium.

Maybe it rose 8%. Maybe it rose 18%. Maybe it rose enough to force a serious conversation about changing plans, shifting more cost to employees, or exploring other options. But that one number hides a lot.

A health insurance premium is not just a payment for doctor visits and hospital bills. It is a bundled price that reflects expected medical claims, prescription drug costs, provider network arrangements, the risk of unexpectedly large claims, administrative expenses, taxes and fees, broker compensation, insurer margin, and the need for financial reserves.

In federal rate-review filings, health insurers generally break premiums into broad categories such as projected incurred claims, administrative expenses, taxes and fees, and profit and risk load. Those buckets do not show every detail a business owner might care about, but they are a useful starting point for understanding what is really inside the monthly premium. For small businesses, this matters because health insurance cost is often treated as one unavoidable lump sum. In reality, it is made up of several different pressures. Some are hard for an employer to influence. Others can be affected, at least indirectly, through plan structure, network choice, funding arrangement, and benefits strategy.
Taking a few minutes to read this will provide you with more knowledge than most brokers and help you to take control of your health plan costs.
Premiums Are Built Around Expected Claims
The largest part of a health insurance premium is typically the insurer’s estimate of future healthcare claims.

This means the carrier is projecting how much it expects to pay for covered medical services during the coming plan year. In formal rate-development materials, these projected claims are the foundation on which the rest of the premium is built. Administrative expenses, taxes, fees, and profit or risk charges are added around that expected claims base.

For a small business owner, the simplest way to think about it is: The premium starts with the cost of healthcare the carrier expects to pay, then adds the cost of running and protecting the insurance arrangement and can include several categories.
1. Medical Claims: Hospitals, Doctors, Procedures, and Ongoing Care
The largest visible component inside most health insurance premiums is medical claims. These are the costs tied to covered healthcare services such as:
Hospital stays
Surgeries
Emergency room care
Outpatient procedures
Office visits
Specialist care
Imaging and lab work
Behavioral health services
Ongoing treatment for chronic conditions

Actuarial filings commonly analyze projected claims by categories such as inpatient, outpatient, physician, and prescription drug costs. They also consider utilization (how often members are expected to use those services) and, unit cost (how much those services are expected to cost when used).
This distinction matters. Premiums do not rise only because “people are going to the doctor more.” They can also rise because:
A hospital system charges more for the same procedure
More care shifts to expensive outpatient facilities
Higher-cost imaging or specialty services become more common
Chronic conditions require more ongoing treatment
When small employers think about rising premiums, this is usually the biggest place to start: what healthcare is expected to cost in the market overall.
2. Prescription Drug Costs

Prescription drugs are part of claims, but they deserve their own discussion because they have become one of the most visible and misunderstood pieces of health plan cost. Prescription spending can include:
Common generic medications
Brand-name drugs
Specialty medications
Injectables and biologics
High-cost therapies for complex conditions

In insurer rate-development work, prescription drug claims are often modeled separately from other medical claim categories because drug trend can behave differently from hospital or physician cost trend. For business owners, the practical point is this: A plan can have relatively ordinary doctor and hospital usage, but a small number of high-cost prescriptions can still create meaningful pressure on claim costs.

This is one reason two groups that look similar from a headcount perspective can have very different expected costs under an underwritten arrangement. It is also why prescription drug management, formulary design, and specialty medication exposure often matter in the broader conversation about health plan cost.
3. Provider Network Pricing and Utilization
A health insurance premium is also affected by which providers are in the network and how the plan is designed to direct care.
CMS rate-review instructions explicitly identify the plan’s provider network, delivery system characteristics, and utilization management practices as factors that may affect plan-level pricing.
That may sound abstract, but it has a very practical meaning: The same care can cost very different amounts depending on where it is delivered.

A procedure done at one hospital system may cost much more than the same procedure performed through a different contracted facility. A broad network that includes nearly every major hospital may be attractive to employees, but it can also carry higher costs. A more managed or narrower network may lower expected claims, but it can create access concerns if employees want specific doctors or health systems.
Provider network strategy can influence premiums through:
Negotiated reimbursement rates
Hospital and physician contracting
Access to lower-cost settings of care
Whether the plan steers members toward urgent care, primary care, telehealth, or higher-cost emergency settings
Prior authorization and other utilization-management practices
4. Large-Claim Risk and the Cost of Uncertainty

Health insurance premiums do not reflect only the “average” expected year. They also reflect the possibility of a bad year. A serious cancer diagnosis, a premature birth, a transplant, a major accident, or a complex specialty drug regimen can create claims that dwarf ordinary office visits and routine prescriptions. Fully insured carriers take on that risk when they issue the policy.

Rate-review materials recognize this through concepts such as risk and profit load, risk adjustment, high-cost risk pool adjustments, and other mechanisms used to account for uncertainty and unusually large claims in the broader market. For the employer, this shows up as part of the premium rather than as a separate visible charge and that is an important difference between fully insured and level-funded health plans. In a fully insured plan, the employer sees one bundled premium. The carrier owns the claims risk. In a level-funded plan, the pieces are often more visible: expected claims funding, administrative costs, and stop-loss coverage against large claims.

Either way, protection from unpredictable high-cost claims has a price. The difference is how clearly the employer sees it and whether the employer may later participate in better-than-expected claims experience.
5. Administrative and Operating Costs
Health insurance does not run itself. The insurer also has to pay for the systems and people needed to administer coverage, including:
Claims processing
Eligibility and enrollment
Billing
Customer service
Member portals and technology
Compliance and regulatory reporting
Provider contracting
Utilization review
Care management
Appeals and grievances
Data systems and fraud controls

CMS rate-review materials group these costs under administrative expense, and they are part of the non-claims portion of the premium. Some of these expenses are easy for consumers to criticize. Others are essential. A health insurer that cannot process claims accurately, maintain provider contracts, meet regulatory standards, or support members properly would create a different kind of cost problem.

For small employers, the useful question is not simply: “Why is there administration at all?” It is: “What administrative infrastructure are we paying for, and does the plan structure deliver enough value for the cost?”
6. Broker Compensation, Marketing, and Distribution Costs
Another piece of the premium structure is the cost of distribution.
That can include:
Broker commissions or compensation
Sales support
Proposal systems
Marketing
Enrollment support
Account management

CMS rate instructions refer to distribution and administrative costs as part of the allowable plan-level cost structure. For small business owners, it is worth understanding that advisor compensation is often embedded somewhere in the economics of the health plan, even if it does not appear as a separate invoice.

That does not mean the broker is “adding” an unnecessary layer. A good benefits advisor should help the employer interpret renewals, compare plan structures, understand cost drivers, handle employee questions, avoid poor-fit decisions and coordinate a more thoughtful long-term benefits strategy. But it does mean small businesses should expect real value from the advice they receive.
7. Taxes, Fees, and Assessments

Health insurance premiums can also include taxes, regulatory fees, and other assessments. CMS rate-review instructions break out taxes and fees as a separate component from administrative expenses and profit/risk load. These may vary depending on the market, jurisdiction, and specific regulatory requirements. For the employer, they are not usually controllable in the same way that plan design or network selection may be. But they are still part of why the premium is higher than claims alone.
This is also why a premium should not be interpreted as just “claims plus profit.” There are multiple layers between the cost of care and the final amount billed.
8. Profit, Risk Load, or Contribution to Surplus

Health insurers also price for profit, risk margin, contribution to surplus and the possibility that actual claims or expenses exceed projections CMS rate-review materials label this category profit and risk load.

For a for-profit carrier, some amount of margin is expected. For a nonprofit carrier, the comparable concept may be framed more as a contribution to surplus or financial stability rather than shareholder profit. Either way, the insurer is not merely collecting premium and passing through exact medical costs. It is taking insurance risk and maintaining a viable business.

This is also where the ACA’s Medical Loss Ratio, often called the 80/20 rule in the individual and small-group markets, enters the conversation. In general, carriers in those markets must spend at least 80% of premium revenue on medical care and quality-improvement activities, or issue rebates if they fall short. The remaining share is not pure profit; it covers administration, marketing, distribution, and margin.
9. Reserves, Surplus, and the Ability to Pay Future Claims
Insurance is a promise to pay claims in the future. To make that promise credible, insurers need adequate reserves and surplus.

Reserves are liabilities held for obligations the insurer expects to pay, such as claims that have already occurred but have not yet been fully reported or settled. Surplus provides an additional financial cushion to absorb adverse experience and protect policyholders.

This is not always a clean “line item” inside the premium in the way claims or administrative expenses are. But rates must be sufficient to support the insurer’s broader financial stability over time.

For a small employer, the practical takeaway is simple: Part of what you are buying is not just this month’s healthcare usage. You are buying the carrier’s ability to stand behind the promise when expensive claims hit. That protection has economic value, even though it is easy to overlook during renewal season.
Which Premium Components Can a Small Employer Influence?
This is where the topic becomes useful rather than merely educational.
A small employer usually cannot control:
State and federal fees
The carrier’s basic need for solvency
Broad market medical inflation
Whether someone has a catastrophic diagnosis next year
But an employer may be able to influence or at least evaluate:
Provider network selection
Plan design
Funding structure
Prescription drug management differences between plan options
Whether a level-funded arrangement is worth comparing
Whether current benefits spending aligns with hiring and retention goals
That is why the components matter. They help owners determine What is truly outside their control and what deserves review.
Why This Matters for Small Businesses

For a 12-person engineering firm, a 20-person technology company, or a 35-person trade contractor, health insurance is rarely just an HR line item. It is often one of the largest recurring employee-benefit expenses the company faces.
When premiums increase, the owner may feel like the only choices are: Pay more  |  Cut benefits  |  Shift cost to employees
Sometimes those are the only immediate options but, not always. A clearer understanding of what sits inside the premium can lead to better questions:
Are we paying for a provider network that is broader than employees need?
Are prescription claims or large-claim risk putting pressure on the plan?
Would a different funding structure better reward favorable claims experience?
Are we treating a strategic business expense like a commodity renewal?
Those are much better questions than simply asking for “the cheapest plan.”
The Bottom Line

A small business health insurance premium is made up of more than just medical bills. It generally reflects expected medical claims, prescription drug costs, provider network and utilization patterns, the risk of large unpredictable claims, administrative operations, distribution and broker compensation, taxes and regulatory fees, profit or contribution to surplus and financial stability needs such as reserves and solvency support

Federal rate-review materials organize premiums around claims, administrative expense, taxes and fees, and profit/risk load, but for a business owner, the practical story is broader. Your premium is the price of healthcare, insurance risk, and the system required to deliver both.

Understanding that structure will not make health insurance inexpensive. But it can make the next renewal conversation far more productive and it can help identify which cost pressures are worth exploring more deeply.
FAQ SECTION
1. What are the main components of a health insurance premium?

At a high level, health insurance premiums reflect projected claims, administrative expenses, taxes and fees, and profit or risk load. In practical terms, that includes medical claims, prescriptions, provider network costs, operations, distribution costs, and insurer risk protection.
2. Are medical claims the biggest part of the premium?

Medical and prescription drug claims are typically the core driver of premium development because the insurer begins with projected healthcare costs before adding administrative, tax, and risk-related amounts.
3. Are prescription drugs included in health insurance premiums?
Yes. Prescription drug costs are part of projected claims, and insurers often analyze them separately from inpatient, outpatient, and physician claims when developing rates.
4. How do provider networks affect health insurance premiums?

Provider networks can affect premiums through negotiated prices, delivery system design, and utilization-management practices. CMS rate-review instructions identify provider network and delivery system characteristics as factors that can influence plan-level pricing.
5. Is profit the same as the non-claims portion of premium?

No. In the individual and small-group markets, the ACA Medical Loss Ratio rule generally requires at least 80% of premium revenue to go toward medical care and quality improvement, but the remaining share covers administration, marketing, distribution, and margin — not just profit.
6. Why is there a cost for large claim risk?

Fully insured carriers assume the risk that actual claims may be worse than expected, including very large and unpredictable claims. Premiums account for that uncertainty through broader risk-pricing mechanisms and risk-related loads.
7. Are broker commissions included in health insurance premiums?
Distribution costs, which can include broker compensation and related sales expenses, are part of the broader administrative and distribution cost structure used in health insurance pricing.
8. What parts of the premium can a small business actually influence?

A small employer cannot control every cost driver, but it can often evaluate plan design, provider network, funding structure, and whether alternative arrangements such as level-funded coverage deserve comparison.
In future articles, we'll dive more deeply into the various components and show you meaningful ways you might be able to impact them for your plan.

title: How ACA Influences Small Business Health Insurance Premiums
description: When a small business owner looks at a health insurance renewal, the natural question is: “Why is our rate going up?”

blocks.text: When a small business owner looks at a health insurance renewal, the natural question is: “Why is our rate going up?”

Many owners assume the answer must be tied directly to their own employees’ medical claims. If the group had a good year, they expect a modest renewal. If the group had a bad year, they expect a larger increase. That logic makes sense. But for many fully insured ACA-compliant small-group health plans, it is not exactly how pricing works.

In the ACA small-group market, insurers generally cannot base premiums on a company’s employees’ health status, medical history, gender, or prior claims experience. Instead, premiums are primarily shaped by a narrower set of permitted rating factors, including age, geographic area, tobacco use and family enrollment. That rating system creates more stability and better access for many small employers. But it can also leave business owners confused, especially when their own workforce seems healthier than average yet their premiums remain high.
Understanding how these rates are built is one of the most important first steps in deciding whether your current health plan still makes sense.
What “Small Group” Usually Means

In most states, the ACA small-group market generally applies to employers with 1 to 50 full-time and full-time-equivalent employees, although there are some state-specific differences. For many small businesses in Illinois and Texas (our primary areas of operation), this is the market they are dealing with when they shop for a traditional fully insured group health plan.

This matters because small-group rules are different from large-group rules. Larger employers may have pricing and underwriting structures that look more directly at the group’s own experience. Small employers buying ACA-compliant fully insured coverage operate within a more standardized rating framework.
Before the ACA, Insurers Had More Ways to Price Small Groups

Before the ACA’s market reforms took effect, small-group health insurance underwriting could consider a wider range of factors. Depending on the state and carrier, insurers might look at health conditions, claims history, gender mix, industry, or other characteristics when determining rates. CMS has noted that before 2014, small employer rates could be affected by health status, claims history, gender, occupation, and small employer size.
That old system created major problems.

A small business with one employee facing cancer treatment, a major surgery, or an expensive chronic condition could face steep pricing pressure. Employers with older workforces or employees with known medical issues could also have a harder time finding affordable coverage. The ACA changed that by moving the small-group market toward a more standardized structure. The goal was to make coverage more accessible and prevent insurers from heavily penalizing certain groups based on health conditions or employee demographics.
The Main Factors That Can Affect ACA Small Group Premiums
For ACA-compliant individual and small-group coverage, the permitted rating factors are limited. The most important ones are:

1. Age - Older individuals can be charged more than younger individuals, but the difference is capped. Under federal ACA rules, adult premium variation by age is generally limited to a 3-to-1 ratio, meaning an older adult’s premium cannot be more than three times the premium charged to a younger adult for the same plan and rating area.

2. Geographic Area - Where employees live can affect rates. Healthcare costs, provider prices, local competition, and regional market conditions can differ meaningfully from one area to another. That means a small business in Chicago may see different pricing than a similar business in a smaller Illinois market, and a company in Dallas may see different results than one in rural Texas.

3. Tobacco Use - Insurers may charge more for tobacco users, subject to applicable federal and state rules. Healthcare.gov notes that insurers can charge tobacco users up to 50% more in certain markets, although states may impose different limits.
4. Family Enrollment - Premiums can be higher when coverage includes a spouse or dependents. The total cost of coverage naturally increases as more family members are enrolled.

These factors may sound straightforward, but they explain only part of what business owners feel at renewal time. The biggest surprise often comes from understanding what does not directly affect ACA small-group premiums.
What Cannot Directly Affect ACA Small Group Premiums
For ACA-compliant small-group health insurance, insurers generally cannot directly vary rates based on:
Health status
Pre-existing conditions
Prior claims experience
Gender
Occupation
How long someone has held coverage
The small employer’s size within the small-group market

CMS specifically identified those factors as no longer permitted for premium rating in the small-employer market under the ACA reforms. Healthcare.gov also states that insurers cannot charge men and women different prices for the same plan and cannot take current health or medical history into account when setting premiums.
This is a major shift from how many business owners intuitively think insurance should work.

A group with low claims does not automatically get a low fully insured ACA rate. A group with higher claims is not necessarily singled out for a claims-based renewal in the same way a larger experience-rated group might be. Instead, the employer is participating in a broader small-group market structure.
Why the 3-to-1 Age Rule Matters

The 3-to-1 age rating limit is one of the most important concepts for business owners to understand. In plain English, it means that insurers cannot price older adults at more than three times the rate charged to younger adults for the same plan and area.

That rule is meant to prevent older individuals and groups with older employees from being priced out of coverage. But it also means younger employees bear more of the cost than they would under a pricing model that followed expected medical expenses more closely. This becomes especially important for certain small businesses.

A technology firm in Austin, an engineering firm in suburban Chicago, or a contracting company with a younger field workforce may feel that its workforce demographics should produce especially favorable pricing. Yet in the fully insured ACA small-group market, that advantage is only partly reflected through age rating. Other favorable traits, such as lower expected claims or fewer known health conditions, generally cannot be used directly in the premium.
That is one reason some younger, healthier employers feel disconnected from the rates they receive.
Why Your Own Claims May Not Explain Your Renewal

Small business owners often focus heavily on their own group’s recent claims. That is understandable. Claims feel concrete and it is how other lines of insurance price their renewals. If employees barely used the plan, an owner may expect a low renewal.

But in the ACA fully insured small-group market, your own claims history is generally not the direct pricing engine. Instead, renewal pricing is influenced by the broader rating structure, the carrier’s approved rate changes, the plan selected, the ages and coverage tiers of those enrolled, and the applicable geographic rating area.

That does not mean claims are irrelevant to the overall health insurance system. Carriers still consider broader market experience when pricing products and filing rates. But at the individual small-group employer level, your specific claims are not usually used the same way many owners assume.

This distinction helps explain a frustrating experience many businesses have: “We barely used the plan, but the renewal still increased.” In a fully insured ACA small-group framework, that can happen without anything being wrong.
A Simple Example
Imagine two small employers:
Company A: 16-person engineering firm with: Mostly younger employees, strong participation, few dependents enrolled, little known recent medical activity
Company B: 16-person professional services firm with: Older average employee ages, more family coverage, higher expected healthcare needs

Under ACA small-group rating rules, the rates will not be identical. Age and enrollment structure matter. But Company A’s full health-risk advantage cannot simply be priced directly into the premium, because the insurer generally cannot rate the group based on health status or claims history.
This is where some business owners begin to ask whether a different funding structure, such as a level-funded plan, may be worth comparing.
Where Level-Funded Plans Enter the Conversation
A level-funded health plan is different from a traditional fully insured ACA small-group plan. While the details vary by carrier and state, level-funded arrangements typically combine:
A fixed monthly payment
Administrative costs
Claims funding
Stop-loss protection against unusually high claims

For some employers, especially those with favorable demographics or lower expected claims, level-funded proposals may offer a pricing approach that pays closer attention to the employer’s own risk profile. That is why these plans often come up when a younger or healthier small business begins questioning fully insured ACA rates.
Still, this needs to be said plainly: Level-funded plans are not automatically cheaper nor automatically better.

A level-funded option may look attractive for one small business and not for another. The outcome can depend on the group’s size, employee census, plan design, participation, medical underwriting process where applicable, and the employer’s comfort with the structure being offered.
The smart move is not to assume one funding method is superior. The smart move is to compare them intelligently.
Why This Matters for Illinois and Texas Small Businesses
Small employers in Illinois and Texas are often trying to balance three goals at once:
Keep benefit costs manageable
Offer something strong enough to recruit and retain employees
Avoid unnecessary complexity

Understanding ACA small-group rating rules helps owners make better decisions on all three fronts. If a business has an older workforce, significant medical needs, or simply wants the familiar structure of a traditional fully insured plan, ACA small-group coverage may remain a strong fit.

If a business has a younger or more favorable demographic profile, it may be worth reviewing whether the current rate structure is still the best match. Either way, better understanding leads to better decisions.
What Business Owners Should Review Before Accepting a Renewal
Before simply accepting the next health insurance renewal, a small business owner should understand:
How much of the increase is tied to age changes or plan changes
Whether the current plan design still fits employees’ needs
Whether employee contributions remain sustainable
Whether fully insured alternatives have been compared
Whether a level-funded option is worth evaluating
Whether the current benefit package supports hiring and retention goals

These are not just insurance questions. They are business planning questions. For a small company, even a moderate health plan inefficiency can affect cash flow, compensation decisions, and the ability to compete for talent. And, just the simple act of exploring a level-funded plan (whether you actually move forward with it or not) can provide you with information that shapes your fully-insured plan design as well as strategic HR decisions surrounding your employees.
The Bottom Line

ACA small-group health insurance rates are built around a standardized rating structure. Premiums can generally vary based on age, geography, tobacco use, and family enrollment, but not directly on health status, gender, or prior claims experience.

That framework created important protections and made the small-group market more accessible. But it also means some employers, especially younger and healthier groups, may feel that their rates do not fully reflect their own workforce profile.

For small businesses in Illinois and Texas, understanding how rates are calculated is the first step toward deciding whether the current plan is still the right fit — or whether it is time to compare other options.
FAQ SECTION
1. How are small business health insurance rates calculated under the ACA?

ACA-compliant small-group premiums are generally based on age, geographic area, tobacco use, and family enrollment. Insurers generally cannot directly base premiums on health status, gender, or prior claims history.
2. Do my employees’ claims affect our fully insured small-group renewal?

For ACA-compliant fully insured small-group plans, an employer’s own claims history is generally not used directly in the same way it may be for larger experience-rated groups. Broader market pricing, plan design, enrolled ages, and rating area still matter.
3. Can insurers charge older employees more than younger employees?

Yes, but adult age-based pricing is generally limited to a 3-to-1 ratio under federal ACA rules, meaning the oldest adult rate cannot exceed three times the youngest adult rate for the same plan and rating area.
4. Can men and women be charged different prices for the same ACA small-group plan?
No. Healthcare.gov states that insurers cannot charge men and women different prices for the same plan.
5. Can pre-existing conditions increase a small business’s ACA group premium?
ACA-compliant plans cannot price coverage based on an individual’s current health or medical history in the small-group market.
6. Why would a younger, healthier company compare level-funded plans?

Because fully insured ACA small-group rates generally do not directly reflect the group’s own health status or claims history. Some employers with favorable demographics want to compare whether a different funding structure may be a better fit.
7. Are level-funded plans always better than fully insured ACA plans?
No. Level-funded plans can be worth comparing, but the right fit depends on the employer’s size, employee profile, plan design, participation, and risk tolerance.
8. What should I review before renewing my small business health plan?
Review the renewal increase, employee demographics, plan design, contribution strategy, alternative fully insured plans, and whether a level-funded comparison makes sense for your business.

title: Cross-Purchase v. Entity-Purchase Buy-Sell Agreements
description: For businesses with multiple owners, one of the most important decisions in buy-sell planning is determining how ownership interests will be transferred if an owner dies, becomes disabled, retires, or unexpectedly exits ...

blocks.text: For businesses with multiple owners, one of the most important decisions in buy-sell planning is determining how ownership interests will be transferred if an owner dies, becomes disabled, retires, or unexpectedly exits the business.

Two of the most common structures are cross-purchase agreements and entity-purchase agreements. While both are designed to help facilitate ownership transition and business continuity, they operate differently and may create different administrative, financial, and tax considerations.
For many closely held businesses, understanding the differences between these structures is an important part of long-term planning.
What Is a Cross-Purchase Agreement?
In a cross-purchase agreement, the surviving owners agree to purchase the departing owner’s ownership interest directly.
For example, if a business has three equal owners and one owner dies, the remaining two owners would personally purchase the deceased owner’s share according to the terms of the agreement.
Life insurance is commonly used to fund these arrangements. In many cases, each owner owns policies on the other owners so funds are available to complete the purchase if an owner dies unexpectedly.

Cross-purchase arrangements are often viewed as attractive for businesses with a smaller number of owners because they can provide certain tax basis advantages for the surviving owners. After the purchase, the remaining owners generally receive an increase in basis tied to the acquired ownership interest. However, administration can become more complicated as the number of owners increases. Multiple policies may be required, and managing ownership, premium payments, and policy coordination can become increasingly complex over time.
What Is an Entity-Purchase Agreement?
In an entity-purchase agreement, sometimes called a stock redemption agreement, the business itself agrees to purchase the departing owner’s interest.
Rather than the surviving owners personally buying the ownership share, the company redeems the ownership interest directly.

Under this structure, the business commonly owns the life insurance policies on the owners and receives the proceeds if an owner dies. The business then uses those funds to purchase the departing owner’s interest according to the agreement terms.

Entity-purchase arrangements are often viewed as simpler from an administrative perspective, particularly for businesses with multiple owners. Instead of requiring owners to maintain policies on one another, the business manages the policies centrally. However, depending on the business structure and tax situation, entity-purchase agreements may not provide the same basis adjustment advantages that can exist under certain cross-purchase arrangements.
Why Businesses Evaluate Both Structures

The appropriate structure depends on many factors, including: number of owners, business entity type, ownership percentages, long-term succession goals, administrative preferences, funding strategy and tax considerations
For example, a two-owner engineering firm may evaluate planning differently than a manufacturing company with five owners or a growing contractor business with future ownership transition plans.

In many cases, businesses also evaluate: whether ownership is expected to remain stable, whether future owners may be added, how valuation will be determined, how disability or retirement situations will be handled, and whether the business itself has sufficient liquidity
Because buy-sell planning affects both ownership continuity and long-term business operations, these decisions are often more significant than simply selecting an insurance product.
Why Life Insurance Is Commonly Used
Life insurance is frequently used in both cross-purchase and entity-purchase agreements because it can provide immediate liquidity during an otherwise financially stressful situation.
Without funding in place, surviving owners or the business itself may struggle to:
Purchase ownership interests
Maintain cash flow
Satisfy estate obligations
Preserve operational stability
Insurance funding helps create a mechanism for ownership transfer while reducing financial strain during a difficult transition period.
Planning Considerations Matter

Many businesses postpone buy-sell planning because ownership transitions feel distant or uncomfortable to discuss. However, uncertainty surrounding ownership transfer can create significant operational and financial problems if planning has not been established before a triggering event occurs.
Properly structured agreements help establish the transition procedures, valuation methods, funding and long-term success.
For many closely held businesses, buy-sell planning is less about insurance products and more about reducing uncertainty during one of the most difficult situations a business can face.
Final Thoughts

Both cross-purchase and entity-purchase agreements can provide effective frameworks for ownership continuity when properly structured. The right approach depends on the size of the business, ownership structure, long-term planning goals, and overall succession strategy.

For businesses with multiple owners, evaluating these structures before a major life event occurs can help create greater clarity, stability, and long-term continuity for owners, employees, clients, and family members alike.

title: The Unique Healthcare Challenges Facing Texas Small Businesses
description: Texas businesses operate in one of the most difficult healthcare environments in the country. Rising insurance costs, limited network options, high uninsured rates, and affordability concerns continue placing pressure on...

blocks.text: Texas businesses operate in one of the most difficult healthcare environments in the country. Rising insurance costs, limited network options, high uninsured rates, and affordability concerns continue placing pressure on both employers and employees.
For small businesses trying to recruit and retain workers while managing long-term costs, these challenges increasingly affect hiring, employee satisfaction, and financial planning decisions.
Texas Continues to Have One of the Highest Uninsured Rates in the Country

Texas consistently reports the highest uninsured rate in the United States. According to data from the Kaiser Family Foundation, approximately 19% of Texans remain uninsured, significantly higher than the national average. (kff.org)
This impacts not only individuals, but also employers competing for workers in industries where access to health coverage can influence recruiting and retention decisions.

Businesses without strong healthcare options may find it more difficult to attract experienced employees, particularly in competitive industries such as engineering, construction, manufacturing, and technology.
Healthcare Affordability Remains a Major Concern

Healthcare affordability continues to be a growing issue across Texas. Premiums, deductibles, and out-of-pocket costs have increased steadily over time, placing pressure on both employers and employees.
Recent studies have shown many Texas families spend more than 10% of household income on healthcare-related expenses, including premiums and deductibles. (axios.com)

For small businesses, annual renewal increases often create difficult tradeoffs between maintaining affordable employee contributions, preserving coverage quality, controlling long-term operating costs, and remaining competitive when hiring new employees. Many employers express frustration that rising costs frequently appear disconnected from the actual demographics or utilization patterns of their workforce.
Many Texans Delay or Avoid Medical Care Due to Cost
Cost concerns also affect healthcare utilization. Surveys continue to show that many Texans delay treatment, skip preventive care, or avoid filling prescriptions because of affordability concerns.

When employees postpone care, businesses can experience indirect impacts through increased absenteeism, lower productivity, delayed diagnoses, and higher long-term claims severity. Over time, healthcare affordability challenges can affect both employee wellbeing and overall employer healthcare costs.
Mental Health Access Remains a Significant Issue

Texas also faces ongoing shortages in mental health access. Many counties continue experiencing shortages of mental health professionals, and employees frequently encounter long wait times or limited provider availability.

These challenges increasingly affect workplace productivity, retention, burnout, morale, and disability-related concerns. As a result, provider network access and overall plan design have become increasingly important considerations for employers evaluating health insurance options.
Marketplace Network Limitations Create Additional Frustration

In many parts of Texas, individual marketplace plans are heavily concentrated in HMO and EPO structures, which may limit out-of-network access and reduce provider flexibility compared to broader PPO arrangements.

Employees who are accustomed to PPO flexibility often find marketplace alternatives restrictive, particularly when they travel frequently, rely on specialist care, or want broader physician access. For many employers, maintaining strong provider networks continues to be an important part of recruiting and retaining skilled employees.
Small Businesses Face Difficult Long-Term Decisions
For many Texas employers, healthcare challenges have evolved beyond simple annual premium shopping.

Businesses are increasingly evaluating long-term cost sustainability, PPO network access, workforce demographics, employee retention concerns, funding structure alternatives, and the predictability of future renewals.
This has contributed to growing interest in alternative funding structures such as level-funded health plans, particularly among businesses with approximately 10–50 employees.

While level-funded plans are not appropriate for every business, some employers are exploring whether alternative funding models may better align with their workforce profile and long-term planning goals.
Why These Challenges Matter to Employers

Healthcare costs now influence far more than insurance budgets alone. For many small businesses, employee benefits directly affect recruiting, retention, workplace stability, employee satisfaction, long-term operating costs, and overall business competitiveness.

As healthcare costs and access concerns continue evolving across Texas, employers are increasingly looking for strategies that balance affordability, provider access, and long-term sustainability in a difficult and rapidly changing market.
How Level-Funded Health Plans Are Becoming Part of the Conversation

As healthcare affordability pressures continue growing across Texas, many small businesses are beginning to evaluate whether alternative funding structures may provide more flexibility than traditional fully insured plans or limited-network marketplace options.
One of the primary reasons employers explore level-funded health plans is the potential for broader PPO network access while maintaining more predictable monthly budgeting.

In many areas of Texas, individual market coverage is heavily concentrated in HMO and EPO structures that can limit physician access and out-of-network flexibility. Employees who are accustomed to PPO plans often view network access as an important part of their overall compensation and benefits package.

For employers trying to recruit and retain skilled workers, particularly in industries such as engineering, construction, manufacturing, and professional services, maintaining strong provider access can become an important competitive factor.
Level-funded plans frequently provide access to larger PPO networks while operating under a different funding structure than traditional fully insured small-group plans.

These arrangements combine predictable monthly payments, stop-loss protection, underwriting considerations, and alternative funding mechanics into a structure designed to provide more stable budgeting while evaluating risk differently than traditional community-rated plans.

Rather than relying entirely on broader community-rated pricing structures, level-funded plans may allow pricing to align more closely with certain workforce demographic characteristics and utilization expectations.

For some businesses with favorable workforce profiles, this can create opportunities to evaluate long-term affordability, renewal sustainability, PPO network access, additional cost transparency, and alternative approaches to managing healthcare expenses.

Level-funded plans are not appropriate for every business and do not automatically reduce costs in every situation. Factors such as employee age, participation levels, industry type, geographic location, and historical utilization patterns all influence underwriting and long-term performance.

However, as Texas employers continue facing rising premiums, affordability concerns, and provider network frustrations, level-funded health plans are becoming an increasingly common part of long-term employee benefits discussions for businesses with approximately 10–50 employees.

title: The Expansion of Level-Funded Health Plans

blocks.text: For many years, self-funded health insurance was primarily reserved for large employers. Companies with hundreds or even thousands of employees had enough financial stability to take on the risk of paying employee medical claims directly. Smaller businesses generally stayed in the fully insured market, where the insurance carrier assumed the risk in exchange for fixed monthly premiums.
Over time, that began to change.

As healthcare costs continued to rise and underwriting technology improved, insurance companies and third-party administrators started developing new ways for smaller employers to participate in self-funded arrangements without taking on the same level of financial risk as a large corporation. This led to the growth of what is now commonly referred to as “level-funded” health insurance.

Today, level-funded plans are available to many businesses with as few as five enrolled employees. In some industries and demographic groups, these plans can provide lower costs, additional flexibility, and greater transparency than traditional small-group health insurance.
How Level Funding Works
A level-funded plan combines several components into one monthly payment:
Administrative costs
Expected medical claims
Stop-loss insurance protection

In many cases, employers pay a consistent monthly amount similar to a traditional fully insured plan. However, if claims are lower than expected, some plans may provide surplus refunds at the end of the year.
At the same time, stop-loss protection is designed to limit catastrophic risk for the employer.
This structure helped bring self-funding “down market” from large corporations to smaller businesses.
Why the Market Has Expanded
Several trends have accelerated growth in the level-funded market over the past decade:
Rising fully insured premiums
Improved underwriting analytics
Better stop-loss structures
Increased interest from younger and healthier employer groups

Greater employer interest in plan customization

The market has also evolved beyond traditional insurance carriers. Today, employers can choose between large national carriers, modern technology-focused platforms, and newer alternative funding organizations.

title: What Happens When the Owner Dies Without a Buy-Sell Agreement
description: Many small business owners spend years building successful companies but never fully address one difficult question: What happens if one of the owners unexpectedly dies?

blocks.text: Many small business owners spend years building successful companies but never fully address one difficult question: What happens if one of the owners unexpectedly dies?

For closely held businesses, partnerships, and multi-owner companies, the answer is often far more complicated than people realize. Without a buy-sell agreement in place, ownership transitions can quickly become stressful for surviving partners, employees, and family members.

In many cases, the deceased owner’s shares or ownership interest pass to a spouse, children, or estate. While family members may inherit ownership rights, they may have little interest in participating in the daily operations of the business.
At the same time, surviving owners may suddenly find themselves sharing financial control and decision-making authority with individuals who were never intended to become business partners.
This can create uncertainty regarding:
company valuation
voting rights
profit distributions
management authority
and future ownership structure
The situation can become even more difficult if the business itself does not have enough liquidity to buy out the deceased owner’s interest.

For example, imagine a small engineering firm with three partners. One partner unexpectedly passes away, and their ownership interest transfers to their spouse. The surviving partners may want to retain control of the company, but they may not have immediate access to the cash needed to purchase the deceased partner’s shares.
Without a pre-arranged agreement and funding strategy, the business could face:
disputes over valuation
pressure to borrow money
forced asset sales
operational disruption
or long-term tension between owners and family members
A buy-sell agreement helps establish rules before emotions and financial pressure enter the situation.
These agreements commonly define:
who can purchase ownership interests
when a buyout occurs
how the business is valued
and how the transaction is funded
Funding is one of the most important parts of the discussion.

Many businesses use life insurance as a funding mechanism because it may provide immediate liquidity after an owner’s death. Rather than forcing surviving owners to personally finance a large buyout or liquidate company assets, insurance proceeds can help support a smoother ownership transition.
Buy-sell planning is not only about death. Agreements may also address:
disability
retirement
voluntary exits
divorce
or other triggering events

title: The Reasons Why You Feel You Are Overpaying for Health Insurance
description: Many small business owners are surprised to learn that employee health insurance pricing is not based entirely on the actual health of their own workforce.

blocks.text: Many small business owners are surprised to learn that employee health insurance pricing is not based entirely on the actual health of their own workforce.
In fact, under current ACA small-group rules, insurance carriers have far fewer ways to price plans than they did prior to the Affordable Care Act.
Before the ACA, small-group underwriting often considered factors such as:
medical history,
gender,
industry,
prescription usage,
and prior claims experience.
Today, small-group pricing is generally much more standardized. In most ACA small-group markets, rates are primarily based on:
age,
geographic location,
tobacco status,
and family composition.

This change helped expand access to coverage and prevented employers from being heavily penalized for serious medical conditions within their workforce. However, it also changed how insurance costs are distributed across the market.
As a result, some employers believe their workforce demographics may cause them to subsidize higher-risk populations within the broader insurance pool.
For example, under ACA rules:
men and women of the same age are generally charged the same premium,
individuals with significant medical conditions typically pay the same as healthier individuals,
and older employees cannot be charged more than three times the rate of younger employees.
This last point is particularly important.

Healthcare costs often increase significantly with age. In many cases, older individuals may use substantially more healthcare services than younger employees. However, because ACA rules limit age-based pricing differences, younger groups may effectively pay more relative to their expected claims costs in order to help stabilize pricing across the broader market.
To simplify the concept:
a healthy 26-year-old employee may cost nearly as much as someone much older despite typically using fewer healthcare services,
and a workforce with very few medical claims may still pay rates influenced by the broader community pool.
This does not mean the ACA is “bad” or that community rating lacks benefits. The system was designed to improve access and reduce pricing discrimination based on health status or medical history.

However, it does help explain why some small employers, particularly those with younger, healthier, or predominantly male workforces, sometimes begin exploring alternatives such as level-funded health plans.

Level-funded arrangements operate differently than traditional ACA community-rated plans. While they still include important protections such as stop-loss insurance, they may allow certain groups to have pricing that is more reflective of their own workforce characteristics and risk profile.

These plans are not appropriate for every employer, and they can involve additional underwriting requirements, participation rules, and eligibility considerations. Businesses with older populations, ongoing high claims activity, or certain medical conditions may not see the same advantages.
Still, for some employers, understanding how demographic factors interact with ACA rating rules provides valuable context when evaluating health insurance strategy.
Rather than viewing annual increases as random or unavoidable, businesses may benefit from taking a broader look at:
workforce demographics,
contribution strategies,
participation levels,
dependent enrollment,
and alternative funding structures.
In some cases, that analysis may confirm that a traditional fully insured plan remains the best fit. In others, it may reveal opportunities worth further exploration.

title: Setting Up Your First Health Plan: Small Business Q&A
description: Thinking about offering health insurance for the first time? You’re not alone. Many small business owners reach the point where benefits aren’t just “nice to have”, they’re a must for attracting and keeping great employe...

blocks.text: Thinking about offering health insurance for the first time? You’re not alone. Many small business owners reach the point where benefits aren’t just “nice to have”, they’re a must for attracting and keeping great employees. But we know the process can feel confusing. Below are answers to the most common questions small business owners ask.
Q: Why should I even offer health insurance? Isn’t it too expensive?

A: Offering health benefits is one of the best ways to stand out as an employer. Most employees consider health insurance their top requested benefit. And here’s something many business owners don’t realize: health insurance can actually be less expensive than giving the same amount in wages.

Here’s why: every dollar of wages is subject to payroll taxes (FICA, unemployment insurance, etc.), but money you put toward health insurance premiums is not. That means you save on payroll taxes, and your employees save too, since they’re getting health coverage with pre-tax dollars instead of paying out of pocket.
Q: How much does it usually cost?

A: Costs depend on your workforce and the plan you choose, but on average, small businesses spend around $6,500 - $7,000 per employee per year. That number can vary wildly depending on the type of plan you select and the age of your employees. You’ll decide how much the company contributes vs. what employees pay. The minimum employer contribution is 50% of the premium but most contribute around 80% - 85%.
Q: What types of plans are available to a small business like mine?
A: You have three main options:
Fully insured plans: The simplest option with predictable monthly premiums, less paperwork.
Level-funded plans: Good for younger/healthier workforces, often lower cost, with potential refunds if claims are low.
ICHRA (Individual Coverage HRA): You set a budget, and employees buy their own coverage. Very flexible.
Q: What do I need to get started?
A: The basics are:
Your business tax ID, SIC code and number of employees.
An employee “census” (ages, zip codes, genders and dependent info, but no health details).
Your budget or how much you’re willing to contribute per employee or per plan.
Once you have that, a broker or consultant can shop plans and present you with options.
Q: How long does it take to set up a plan?

A: Give it at least 30 days if you want it to be a smooth process. You'll need to submit an application and a lot of supporting documentation to the insurance carrier so they can verify that you are a legitimate business with actual employees. This can include but is not limited to: Latest wage and tax filing, SS4 (EIN) document, business license, articles of incorporation, individual applications / waivers for coverage, company application and more.
Q: Do I have to offer the same plan to everyone?

A: Not necessarily. Some businesses offer one plan, others give employees a choice of two or three (for example, a lower-cost high-deductible plan and a richer PPO). The right number depends on your budget and how much choice you want to provide.
Q: How do employees sign up?

A: Many small businesses still use paper enrollment forms submitted to the carrier although most carriers and brokers provide an online enrollment portal. Employees can compare plans side by side, see what their paycheck contributions would be, and enroll electronically. Clear communication is key here. Make sure employees understand the trade-offs between cost and coverage.
Q: Are there compliance requirements I need to worry about?

A: Yes. If you have employees, you know there are hundreds of different federal and state employment laws you have to be careful not to violate. For health benefits, the two most people are concerned with are based on your size:
Under 50 employees: Generally, you’re not required to offer coverage, but you must follow basic rules under ERISA.

50+ employees: You’ll need to meet ACA requirements.
There may also be small annual fees (like the PCORI fee) and state-specific requirements, which your broker can help with.
Q: Bottom line — is it worth it?

A: Absolutely. Beyond the payroll tax savings, offering health benefits makes you more competitive in hiring, improves retention, and shows employees you’re invested in them. For many small businesses, this step marks the transition from being just a workplace to being an employer of choice.
👉 Next step: Gather your employee census and set a budget. With those two pieces, you’ll have everything you need to start shopping for plans.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Understanding Health Insurance
description: Health insurance is an integral part of modern life, providing a safety net against unpredictable medical expenses. As healthcare costs continue to rise, having a comprehensive understanding of health insurance is crucia...

blocks.text: Health insurance is an integral part of modern life, providing a safety net against unpredictable medical expenses. As healthcare costs continue to rise, having a comprehensive understanding of health insurance is crucial for both individuals and businesses. This guide delves deep into the essentials of health insurance, empowering readers to make informed decisions about their coverage.
What is Health Insurance and Why Does It Matter?

Health insurance is a contractual agreement between an individual and an insurance provider, designed to cover a variety of medical expenses. These plans not only provide financial protection but also ensure timely access to healthcare services. For residents and businesses in Barrington, Illinois, understanding how health insurance works is particularly important due to the regional healthcare landscape.
How Does Health Insurance Work?
Health insurance operates on a cost-sharing model where policyholders pay premiums, deductibles, and co-insurance. Here’s a breakdown of key terms:
Premiums: Monthly payments to maintain the insurance policy.
Deductibles: The amount you pay out-of-pocket before insurance coverage begins.
Co-insurance: The percentage of costs shared between you and the insurer after meeting the deductible.
Out-of-pocket Maximum: The maximum amount you’ll pay in a year, after which insurance covers 100% of eligible expenses.
Types of Health Insurance Plans
1. Health Maintenance Organization (HMO)
HMOs focus on in-network care and typically require referrals for specialists. These plans are cost-effective but limit provider options.
2. Preferred Provider Organization (PPO)
PPOs offer flexibility by allowing policyholders to see out-of-network providers, albeit at a higher cost.
3. Exclusive Provider Organization (EPO)
EPOs blend features of HMOs and PPOs, emphasizing in-network care without requiring referrals.
4. High-Deductible Health Plans (HDHP) with Health Savings Accounts (HSAs)
HDHPs are paired with HSAs, enabling policyholders to save for medical expenses on a tax-advantaged basis.
5. Point of Service (POS) Plans
POS plans require policyholders to choose a primary care physician and obtain referrals for specialist care.
Key Factors to Consider When Choosing a Plan
Selecting the right health insurance plan involves balancing coverage and cost. Here are some factors to weigh:
Network Providers: Ensure your preferred doctors and hospitals are in-network.
Prescription Coverage: Check if your medications are included.
Additional Benefits: Look for wellness programs, mental health coverage, and telemedicine options.
Budget: Evaluate premiums, deductibles, and out-of-pocket maximums.
Navigating Health Insurance Challenges
Understanding Terminology
Many find health insurance jargon confusing. Familiarizing yourself with terms like premiums, deductibles, and co-insurance can simplify decision-making.
Comparing Plans
Use online tools or consult with experts to compare plan features and costs effectively.
Managing Costs
Explore high-deductible plans if you’re healthy or infrequent in healthcare usage, and consider subsidies or employer-sponsored options.
Health Insurance Tips for Barrington, Illinois Residents
Explore Local Providers: Research healthcare networks available in the Barrington area.
Leverage State Resources: Illinois residents can access state exchanges for affordable options.
Stay Informed: Keep up with policy changes and updates that could affect coverage.
FAQs About Health Insurance
1. What is the difference between a premium and a deductible?
A premium is the monthly amount paid for insurance, while a deductible is the out-of-pocket amount paid before insurance coverage kicks in.
2. How can I reduce my health insurance costs?
Choose high-deductible plans, utilize HSAs, and compare options annually.
3. Are all preventive services covered by insurance?
Most plans cover preventive services like vaccinations and screenings at no additional cost.
4. Can I switch plans outside of open enrollment?
Yes, if you experience a qualifying life event such as marriage, childbirth, or job loss.
5. How do I find a plan that includes my current doctor?
Consult your doctor’s office or use the insurer’s provider directory to verify network participation.

By understanding the nuances of health insurance and evaluating your unique needs, you can secure a plan that provides both financial protection and access to quality care. Whether you're an individual or a business owner, making informed decisions ensures peace of mind and comprehensive coverage.

title: 5 Ways Small Businesses Cut Health Insurance Costs
description: Small business health insurance doesn’t have to break the bank. By using a few smart strategies, you can save money while keeping your employees happy and healthy. Here’s how:

blocks.text: Small business health insurance doesn’t have to break the bank. By using a few smart strategies, you can save money while keeping your employees happy and healthy. Here’s how:
Group Purchasing Power: Team up with other small businesses to negotiate better rates and lower premiums.
Tax Benefits and Credits: Deduct health insurance costs and claim the Small Business Health Care Tax Credit to save up to 50% on premiums.
Preventive Care and Wellness Programs: Encourage regular checkups and healthy habits to reduce long-term medical costs and employee absenteeism.
High Deductible Health Plans (HDHPs) with Health Savings Accounts (HSAs): Lower premiums and give employees more control over healthcare spending with tax-free savings accounts.
Custom Plan Design: Tailor coverage options to meet your team’s needs while managing costs effectively.

These methods not only reduce expenses but also improve employee satisfaction and retention. If you’re unsure where to start, consulting with experts can help you make the most of these opportunities.
Popular health insurance alternatives for small businesses
1. Use Group Purchasing Power

Small businesses often face challenges in securing affordable insurance because insurers prefer larger groups with predictable risk profiles. But by coming together and leveraging group purchasing power, smaller businesses can negotiate better rates.
"Group purchasing is a way for smaller businesses to use collective purchasing power to secure lower prices." - Horton Group [1]

Instead of tackling the insurance market solo, small businesses can pool their resources to create a larger risk group. This approach makes them more attractive to insurers, leading to reduced rates and improved contract terms.
How Group Plans Benefit Small Businesses

When employees from multiple small businesses are grouped together, insurers can evaluate risk more evenly. This reduces the financial burden of unexpected, high-cost claims by spreading the risk across a larger pool. The result? More predictable claims costs and often substantial savings compared to purchasing coverage individually.

Group Purchasing Organizations (GPOs) play a key role in this process. They negotiate on behalf of their members, using the combined buying power of the group to secure discounted rates and pre-arranged contracts. This gives smaller businesses access to the kind of deals typically reserved for large corporations [2][3].
For health insurance, captives and PEOs are how small businesses realize savings.
Consultants Make Group Plans Easier
Navigating group purchasing options can feel overwhelming, but specialized consultants can simplify the process.

Experts at DWAI Consulting specialize in helping small businesses identify the best group purchasing opportunities. They analyze your industry, employee needs, and budget to match you with the most suitable arrangements.

From evaluating options to managing enrollment and handling negotiations, DWAI Consulting ensures your business gets the most value out of group plans. Their ongoing support helps maintain cost savings year after year.
Leveraging group purchasing power is a smart starting point for cutting insurance costs and building a more stable benefits strategy.
2. Take Advantage of Tax Benefits and Credits

Offering health insurance to employees isn't just a way to attract and retain talent - it can also bring significant tax savings for your business. These tax benefits can substantially lower your actual costs, making health insurance more affordable than it might seem at first glance.
Understanding how to navigate these tax advantages is key to getting the most out of your investment in employee health benefits.
Federal Tax Benefits for Employers
One of the biggest perks? Health insurance premiums are fully tax-deductible as a business expense. This means every dollar spent on premiums directly reduces your taxable income.
Here’s a quick example: If your business spends $50,000 on health insurance premiums and you’re taxed at a 25% rate, you’ll save $12,500 in taxes. That brings your real cost down to $37,500.

This deduction isn’t just for employees - it also applies to premiums paid for their families. And if you’re self-employed, you can deduct your health insurance premiums “above the line,” which lowers your adjusted gross income.
Small Business Health Care Tax Credit
The Small Business Health Care Tax Credit offers even more savings. Unlike deductions, this credit directly reduces the amount of tax you owe, dollar for dollar.
To qualify, your business must:
Employ fewer than 25 full-time employees
Pay average wages below $64,000
Cover at least 50% of employee premiums
Purchase a plan through the Small Business Health Options Program (SHOP) marketplace

If you meet these requirements, the credit can cover up to 50% of premiums paid for small businesses and 35% for tax-exempt organizations. The credit gradually decreases as your employee count or average wages approach the upper limits. However, businesses with 10 or fewer employees earning average wages of $29,000 or less may qualify for the full credit percentage. Even a partial credit can lead to meaningful savings.
Expert Guidance for Maximum Savings

Navigating the tax code can be tricky, but it’s worth it to ensure you’re taking full advantage of these benefits. Companies like DWAI Consulting specialize in helping businesses claim all available tax advantages. They can guide you through the complexities of tax compliance, helping you structure your health insurance program to maximize both savings and employee satisfaction. By tapping into their expertise, you can uncover additional cost-saving opportunities while building a benefits strategy that works for everyone.
3. Focus on Preventive Care and Wellness Programs

Taking care of employee health isn’t just good for morale - it’s a smart way to save on costs. Preventive care and wellness initiatives can help employees stay healthier, which, in turn, reduces medical claims and keeps insurance premium rates more consistent over time. This forward-thinking approach ties in perfectly with other cost-saving strategies discussed throughout this guide.

By tackling health issues early - through regular checkups, screenings, and vaccinations - you can avoid expensive treatments down the road. Insurers often reward lower claim rates with more predictable premiums, making this a win-win for both employers and employees.

Thanks to provisions in the Affordable Care Act, many health insurance plans now cover preventive services without requiring a deductible. This means employees can access flu shots, colonoscopies, blood pressure checks, and other essential screenings without paying out of pocket. Beyond cutting direct medical costs, preventive care also helps reduce absenteeism, keeping your workforce both healthy and productive.
Examples of Low-Cost Wellness Programs

Wellness programs are another practical way to promote health and save money - no massive budget required. These initiatives not only complement preventive care but can also make a noticeable difference in employee well-being and insurance costs.

Simple ideas like fitness challenges or step competitions can motivate employees to stay active. Smoking cessation programs can tackle tobacco-related health concerns, while mental health resources, such as employee assistance programs, offer affordable ways to address workplace stress.

You can also bring health services directly to your team. For example, consider offering on-site screenings or hosting nutrition workshops. Stocking healthier snack options in the break room is another small but effective step toward promoting better eating habits.

Start with manageable, easy-to-track programs and build from there as participation grows. Monitoring engagement and overall health trends can give you a clear picture of how these efforts are impacting both employee wellness and insurance costs. And when leadership gets involved, it often inspires a broader shift toward prioritizing health, creating a ripple effect that benefits the entire organization.
4. Use High Deductible Health Plans (HDHPs) with Health Savings Accounts (HSAs)

Pairing High Deductible Health Plans (HDHPs) with Health Savings Accounts (HSAs) can lower healthcare costs while giving employees greater control over their medical expenses. This setup not only reduces monthly premiums but also offers long-term financial advantages that can positively impact your business's bottom line.

The primary appeal of HDHPs is their lower monthly premiums compared to traditional health plans. For small businesses working within tight budgets, these reduced premiums can free up funds for other essential needs. When combined with an HSA, this option becomes more than just a cost-cutting measure - it turns into a financial tool that benefits both employers and employees.
What Are HDHPs and HSAs?

An HDHP is a health insurance plan with a higher deductible than traditional plans. According to the IRS, for 2025, an HDHP must have a minimum deductible of $1,650 for individual coverage and $3,300 for family coverage, with maximum out-of-pocket limits of $8,300 for individuals and $16,600 for families.

HSAs complement HDHPs by serving as specialized savings accounts for medical expenses. Both employers and employees can contribute to these accounts, and the funds roll over indefinitely - they never expire. Unlike flexible spending accounts, which follow a "use it or lose it" rule, HSAs belong to the employee, even if they leave the company.

For employers, the premium savings from HDHPs can amount to thousands of dollars annually per employee. Employees, on the other hand, benefit from having an account that not only covers medical expenses but also grows over time. This combination encourages smarter healthcare spending, as employees are more likely to compare prices and assess the necessity of certain procedures when using their own money.
Beyond immediate savings, this approach also provides substantial tax advantages, as outlined below.
Tax Benefits of HSAs
HSAs offer a rare triple tax advantage, making them a highly attractive option for both employees and employers.

Tax-deductible contributions: Employer contributions to HSAs are fully deductible as a business expense. Employees also benefit by reducing their taxable income dollar-for-dollar with their contributions. In 2025, contribution limits are set at $4,300 for individual coverage and $8,550 for family coverage, with an additional $1,000 catch-up contribution for employees aged 55 and older.

Tax-free growth: Unlike traditional savings accounts, HSA funds can be invested in options like mutual funds and stocks. Any earnings, dividends, or capital gains grow tax-free, turning the HSA into a long-term savings tool.

Tax-free withdrawals for medical expenses: Employees can use HSA funds for a wide range of qualified medical expenses - doctor visits, prescriptions, dental care, and even some alternative treatments - without paying taxes on the withdrawals. This also applies to items not typically covered by insurance, such as certain over-the-counter medications and medical equipment.

The tax savings add up quickly. For example, an employee in the 22% tax bracket who maximizes their HSA contribution saves $946 annually in federal taxes for individual coverage or $1,881 for family coverage. When you include state taxes and potential FICA savings, the total tax benefit for families often exceeds $2,000 per year.

For employers, contributing to HSAs offers the same tax advantages as traditional health insurance premiums but often at a much lower overall cost. Many small businesses find they can contribute between $1,000 and $2,000 per employee while still spending less than they would on a traditional low-deductible plan.

HSAs are especially appealing to younger, healthier employees due to their long-term savings potential. After age 65, HSA funds can be used for any purpose, functioning like a traditional IRA, though non-medical withdrawals are subject to income tax. This flexibility, combined with tax-free medical withdrawals, makes HSAs a smart choice for building financial security over a lifetime.
5. Customize Plan Design and Payment Strategies

To make the most of your health insurance investment, it's crucial to shape your offerings around your employees' specific needs. By combining group and tax savings with a carefully tailored plan design, you can take cost control to the next level.

Start by getting a clear picture of your workforce's healthcare habits and financial priorities. For instance, a tech startup with younger employees will likely have very different needs compared to a manufacturing company with an older workforce. This kind of targeted planning ensures you're directing resources toward benefits employees will actually use, avoiding unnecessary spending on services that go untouched.
Match Plan Options to Employee Needs
Your workforce isn't one-size-fits-all, and your health plans shouldn't be either. By analyzing demographics and healthcare usage, you can tailor options to better serve your team.
For example:
Younger employees may prefer high-deductible plans that keep premiums low but cover unexpected expenses.
Older employees or those with chronic conditions might benefit from plans with lower deductibles and broader provider networks.

Additionally, consider local provider availability when designing your network options. Narrow network plans, which focus on a smaller range of providers, can often reduce premiums - especially in areas with quality hospital systems.

Offering multiple plan options is another way to meet diverse needs. Include choices like cost-conscious plans with higher deductibles alongside more comprehensive plans with lower out-of-pocket costs. This flexibility allows employees to pick coverage that fits their personal circumstances.
Split Premium Costs Between Employer and Employee

Sharing premium costs is a smart way to balance affordability and manage expenses. For instance, you might cover a larger portion of individual premiums while adjusting family contributions to reflect the higher costs of covering dependents. This approach keeps benefits affordable for employees while maintaining predictable costs for your business.

You can also explore tiered, defined, or salary-based contribution models to align cost-sharing with your broader financial strategy. These methods complement other savings tactics and give you more control over benefit expenses.
Compare Costs Across Plan Types

A thorough cost comparison is essential when choosing plan options. Look at factors like monthly premiums, deductibles, cost-sharing structures, and out-of-pocket maximums to find the right balance between affordability and comprehensive coverage.
For example:
High-deductible health plans (HDHPs) paired with health savings accounts (HSAs) often come with lower premiums but require employees to cover more upfront costs.
Preferred provider organization (PPO) plans may have higher premiums but offer more predictable expenses, which some employees may prefer.
By evaluating these variables, you can select plans that align with both your budget and your employees' needs.
