Conclusion: Put These Cost-Saving Methods to Work with Expert Help

Small business health insurance doesn’t have to feel like a financial burden. The five strategies we’ve discussed - harnessing group purchasing power, taking full advantage of tax benefits and credits, promoting preventive care, leveraging HDHPs with HSAs, and tailoring plan designs - can lead to meaningful savings when applied thoughtfully.

These savings aren’t just hypothetical; they’re backed by real numbers. For instance, businesses eligible for the Small Business Health Care Tax Credit can save up to 50% of premium costs [7]. Companies that transition to level-funded health plans often reduce premiums by 5% to 10% and may even receive partial refunds if claims fall below expectations [5]. Considering that the average annual cost of employer-sponsored family coverage is now $21,827 (according to the Kaiser Family Foundation) [6], these strategies could save your business thousands of dollars each year.

That said, navigating the complexities of health insurance isn’t always straightforward. Many small businesses stick with the same provider year after year, potentially missing out on better rates or more suitable coverage options [7]. With the healthcare landscape constantly evolving - thanks to new funding models, tax-advantaged accounts, and regulatory shifts - it’s easy to feel overwhelmed. This is where expert guidance becomes invaluable.

Professional consultants can help you compare carriers objectively, find cost-effective solutions tailored to your needs, and ensure you remain compliant with regulations [4][5]. Their expertise can transform health insurance from a daunting expense into a strategic advantage.

FAQs
How can small businesses use group purchasing power to lower health insurance costs?

Small businesses have a smart way to cut down on health insurance costs: group purchasing power. By joining purchasing groups (PEOs, captives) or associations, multiple businesses can pool their resources to negotiate better deals with insurance providers. This collective approach often leads to lower premiums and improved coverage options.

Another effective tactic is joining associations that have a multiple employer welfare arrangement (MEWA). These can make it easier to access affordable plans that still offer solid coverage. These strategies not only help businesses save money but also ensure employees receive quality benefits, which can go a long way in boosting satisfaction and retention.
What are the eligibility requirements for the Small Business Health Care Tax Credit, and how can small businesses take full advantage of it?
To qualify for the Small Business Health Care Tax Credit, your business needs to meet a few specific requirements:
Employ fewer than 25 full-time workers
Pay an average annual wage of $56,000 or less per employee
Cover at least 50% of health insurance premiums for full-time employees
Provide health coverage through the Small Business Health Options Program (SHOP)

Meeting these criteria can make a big difference for your business. The tax credit can cover up to 50% of your premium costs, helping you save money while offering meaningful benefits to your team. It's not just about cutting expenses - it’s also a smart way to enhance employee satisfaction.
What are the benefits of pairing a High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) with a Health Savings Account (HSA) for small businesses and their employees?

Pairing a High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) with a Health Savings Account (HSA) can be a smart move for small businesses and their employees. For employers, HDHPs often come with lower premiums, which can help cut down overall healthcare expenses. Plus, any contributions made to employees' HSAs are tax-deductible, adding another layer of financial benefit.

For employees, the perks are just as appealing. They can make tax-free contributions to their HSA, use those funds for qualified medical expenses, and even save for future healthcare needs. The best part? HSA funds grow tax-free and stay with employees, even if they switch jobs, offering long-term financial peace of mind. This setup not only promotes more thoughtful healthcare spending but also helps both employers and employees keep costs under control.

Compared to other countries with public healthcare systems, the U.S. workplace has uniquely high expectations when it comes to employer-provided benefits. Especially health coverage.

In this post, we’ll break down what U.S. employees typically expect, how those expectations differ from employees in other parts of the world, and how international employers can meet those expectations without overspending.
U.S. Workers Expect Health Coverage to Be the Norm

In many countries, access to healthcare is guaranteed regardless of employment. That’s not the case in the United States. Here, the majority of people under 65 rely on their employer for health insurance.
This leads to three key expectations:

Coverage should start quickly.
     Employees often expect eligibility on day one or within the first 30 days of employment.

The employer pays most of the cost.
     While employees typically contribute to premiums, they expect the employer to cover a significant portion—often 70% or more of the cost for the employee and at least some portion for dependents.

Benefits are part of compensation.
     U.S. workers view benefits as part of their total pay, not a bonus. Weak or confusing benefit options can lower the perceived value of the job.
Beyond Health: What Else U.S. Employees Want
While health insurance is the centerpiece, a strong benefits package often includes:
Dental and vision insurance
Life and disability coverage
Retirement plans like a 401(k)
Health Savings Accounts (HSAs) or Flexible Spending Accounts (FSAs)
Paid time off policies that are clearly defined
Each of these plays a role in creating a competitive total compensation package.
Key Differences: U.S. vs. Global Expectations

title: Tax Advantages of Offering Employee Benefits for Global Employers
description: For international companies employing staff in the United States offering employee benefits (health insurance and retirement plans) isn’t just a way to stay competitive, it can also be a smart financial decision. U.S. ta...

blocks.text: For international companies employing staff in the United States offering employee benefits (health insurance and retirement plans) isn’t just a way to stay competitive, it can also be a smart financial decision. U.S. tax law provides significant advantages for employers who offer health benefits and retirement plans, helping reduce overall payroll tax liability while improving employee satisfaction.
In this post, we’ll break down the key tax benefits for non-U.S. employers offering employee benefits.
Why Tax Treatment Matters in the U.S.

Unlike many countries with government-funded healthcare and pension systems, the U.S. encourages employer-sponsored insurance and retirement planning through the tax code. Health benefits and retirement contributions, when properly structured, are excluded from both employer payroll taxes and employee income taxes, making them one of the most tax-efficient forms of compensation.
Employer Tax Advantages
1.	Payroll Tax Savings

Every dollar your company pays employees in wages is subject to various payroll taxes and expenses for the business. Employer contributions to health insurance and retirement however are excluded from federal income tax, state income tax, social security, medicare, state unemployment insurance and federal unemployment taxes (FUTA). This can lower your total employment costs significantly per dollar contributed and provide employees with greater overall compensation.
2.	Deductible Business Expense

Health insurance premiums, retirement plan administration costs and retirement plan contributions paid by the company are tax-deductible as an ordinary business expense - reducing your corporate tax liability while retirement plans also qualify the business for additional tax credits under the SECURE Act.
3.	Reduced Workers’ Compensation Premiums

Though not a tax it can be thought of one since most states mandate this coverage for workplace incidents. In many cases, we see significantly fewer workers compensation claims in companies with comprehensive health coverage. It's assumed that since employees have health coverage, they are less likely to fake on the job injuries in order to get medical coverage. Also, health insurance premiums and retirement contributions are not included in wage calculations so they are not included in the calcuations for workers compensation rates.
Employee Tax Advantages
1.	Tax-Free Benefit

Employees do not pay federal income, state income nor payroll taxes (listed above) on employer-paid health premiums and retirement contributions. This increases their overall compensation without increasing taxable income.
2.	HSA & FSA Accounts
When paired with the right plan, employees can set aside pre-tax dollars for medical expenses which gives them more take-home value with less cost to the employer.
Considerations for Global Employers
•	Entity Structure Matters: To take full advantage of U.S. tax benefits, your company may need to establish a U.S. entity.
•	Document Compliance: ERISA, ACA, IRS and state regulations require plan documentation and employee notices to preserve tax-favored treatment.
•	Avoid Misclassification: Health plans should not be treated as cash equivalents.

•	Budget Expectations - Company does NOT Pay For 100%: Company health plan contributions rarely cover 100% of the total cost. 80% to 85% for employee only coverage and about 70% for family coverage is the average as of the writing of this article. Retirement plan contributions hover around 4% to 5% of wages.

•	Think in Terms of Total Compensation: U.S. employees think of thier compensation as a combination of wages and other employee benefits. Since the US tax code incentivizes businesses to provide benefits with expense deductions and tax credits, shifting a percentage of the overall compensation budget to benefits can provide more value for employees at a lower net cost to the business.

title: Demystifying Life Insurance Options for Employees
description: Life insurance is one of the most common, yet least understood, benefits offered by employers. While many employees appreciate that coverage exists, few fully understand their options or how to choose the right one. As a...

blocks.text: Life insurance is one of the most common, yet least understood, benefits offered by employers. While many employees appreciate that coverage exists, few fully understand their options or how to choose the right one. As an employer, demystifying life insurance can boost perceived value and employee peace of mind.
Group Term Life Insurance

This is the most common employer-provided benefit. It typically offers a flat amount or a multiple of salary (e.g., 1x or 2x annual pay) and is often provided at no cost to employees. However, it usually ends when the employee leaves the company. As of the date of this writing, many small employers limit the coverage they pay on behalf of employees to $50,000 because these premiums are excluded from an employee’s federal taxable income. Premiums for coverage exceeding $50,000 are considered taxable income and are subject to Social Security and Medicare taxes.
Voluntary Life Insurance

Because $50,000 worth of coverage may not be enough, employers often provide employees the option to buy additional coverage on their own. This may be portable and can sometimes cover spouses and children. Rates are group-based and depending on the amount of coverage, can be written as guaranteed issue (without medical exams).
Permanent Life Insurance as a Benefit

Less common but growing in use among executive teams, permanent policies like whole or universal life can accumulate cash value and be used in executive bonus or split-dollar arrangements. These are valuable tools for retention, wealth planning, and offering long-term incentives that align executive interests with the company’s success.
Convertible Options
Good plans include a convertibility feature, allowing employees to switch to an individual policy when they leave the company which is an important consideration for employees with health concerns.
Employee Education and Access to Expertise is Key
No matter what coverage is offered, it's important to educate employees. Host workshops, provide benefit statements, and offer one-on-one guidance with experts so that employees understand:
How much coverage they need
How their age and health affect cost
The difference between term and permanent insurance
Access to experts that can help them with additional planning needs outside of the company offerings
Final Thoughts

Life insurance is more than a checkbox benefit. With the right mix of coverage options and education, it becomes a meaningful part of your employees' financial safety net — and a differentiator in your overall benefits strategy.

blocks.text: In today’s competitive hiring environment, employee benefits are no longer optional, they are a necessity. You don’t need a Fortune 500 budget to offer meaningful perks that attract and retain top talent. With the right strategy, you can design a cost-effective benefits package that delivers real value to both your team and your bottom line.
Start With What Matters Most to Your Employees

Every workforce is different so don't just assume everyone wants a health plan. Many times your employees already have that covered. Take time to understand what your team actually values. Older workers might prioritize health coverage and younger employees student loan assistance or paid time off.
Tip: Send out an anonymous survey asking employees to rank benefits by importance. You may be surprised by the results and it could save you money by focusing on what really matters.
Explore Ancillary Benefits

Ancillary benefits, such as dental, vision, life insurance, and disability coverage, are low-cost to the employer and can provide enourmous value for employees. You can add multiple benefits at a fraction of the cost of a health plan and it's a great way to get started.
Explore Health Plan Alternatives
If traditional group health insurance is out of your budget, consider options like:
Level-Funded Health Plans – Hybrid plans with predictable costs and the potential for year-end refunds.
ICHRA (Individual Coverage HRA) – Employers reimburse employees for individual health insurance plans.
Health Sharing Plans – Not insurance, but may appeal to some employees as a cost-saving alternative.
Each option has trade-offs, so working with a benefits advisor can help ensure compliance and alignment with your workforce.
Offer Flexible Work Arrangements

Flexibility is one of the most cost-effective benefits you can offer. Remote work, flexible hours, and compressed workweeks cost little or nothing but greatly enhance employee satisfaction and retention.
Provide Financial Wellness Tools

Financial stress affects productivity. Even basic offerings like access to a financial coach, budgeting tools, or workshops can make a big difference. Some platforms offer these services at low or no cost through retirement plan vendors or EAPs. These are often included as free value-adds with some life insurance, health or disability insurance offerings depending on the carrier
Educate and Communicate

A great benefits package is only effective if your employees understand it. Provide clear explanations, hold Q&A sessions, and use visual guides to help them take full advantage of what you offer. Better engagement equals better ROI. You should also consider providing a total compensation statement to your employees so they can see the tangible value they receive.
Don't Forget Yourself

Most small business owners think of themselves last/ They are so focused on their clients, employees and the growth of their business that they miss out on simple ways to improve the personal value they receive through the business. Adding a simple disability policy, life insurance and a basic retirement plan are very low cost ways to not only improve your hiring and retention efforts but, they are a great way to add expense deductions that lower your taxes while providing more value for yourself.
Final Thoughts

You don’t need to match the benefits of a large corporation to stay competitive. By focusing on what your employees value, using smart plan designs, and emphasizing education, you can build a cost-effective benefits package that supports your team and strengthens your business. title: How to Save on Employee Health Insurance in An Uncertain Economy
description: Don’t Cut Quality - Cut Waste

blocks.text: Don’t Cut Quality - Cut Waste

Let’s face it, when the economy gets shaky, business owners feel it first. Margins shrink. Growth slows. And those “fixed” costs like health insurance? They start to look a lot less fixed once you see what’s possible.

The truth is, many small businesses are overpaying for health insurance, especially under ACA small group plans. And in a tough economy, that kind of waste isn’t just annoying, it’s a threat to your bottom line.
Here’s how you can start saving money without slashing benefits or disappointing your team.
1. Eliminate the Lack of Transparency
If you have fewer than 50 employees, chances are your health plan is working against you in two ways.
First, you might be in a high-risk pool. Even if your team isn’t.

ACA small group rules don’t allow real underwriting. That means your pricing is based on the general market, not your specific employees. So even if your team is young, healthy, and low-risk, you’re subsidizing the other businesses that are incurring higher healthcare costs.
Second, you can’t see how your plan is actually being used.

Small group fully insured plans usually don’t provide claims data, not even to your broker. So, you might be paying for “ghost benefits” no one uses (like acupuncture or rich out-of-network coverage) without even realizing it.
Bottom line: You’re likely overpaying both for who you are and what you’re buying.
What to do:
Consider level-funded plans which allow for more customized options and pricing.
Level-funded plans will provide a quote based on your actual employee demographics and medical needs. You might be shocked at how much you can save.
They also provide claims information that will guide future plan designs.
2. Stop Over-Insuring Your Team

This one’s a silent killer. Most employees don’t hit their deductible, and many don’t even use the plan beyond preventive care. Yet companies are paying for low-deductible, gold-tier PPO plans that go mostly untouched.
Why this matters:
You’re paying high premiums for benefits your team isn’t even using.
Employees might feel like they’re getting better coverage, but the math doesn’t support the cost.
What to try instead:
Offer a higher-deductible plan (or an HSA-eligible option) and fund part of the deductible with an HRA or health savings account.
Pair a leaner medical plan with voluntary benefits (like accident, critical illness, or dental/vision) so employees still feel protected without you footing the full bill.
3. Switch to an ICHRA (Individual Coverage HRA)
An ICHRA lets you give employees tax-free money to buy their own health insurance. You stay out of the insurance business. They get more choice. And you can cap your cost predictably.
Why now:
The individual insurance market is often cheaper, especially in competitive states.
You control the budget. Period.
No more renewals that give you sticker shock.
4. Rethink Your Network: PPO vs. HMO
A lot of businesses pay extra for PPO networks because they sound more flexible. But most employees still stay in-network for cost reasons and many never use the “extra” access they’re paying for.
Ask yourself:
How many employees are actually seeing out-of-network providers?
Would a more structured network (like an HMO or EPO) work just as well or even better?
What to try:
Run a network analysis: See where your employees actually get care and whether they’d be just as well-served by a smaller network.
Consider HMO options that include major hospitals or health systems in your area. The premium savings can be significant.
5. Use a Benefits Strategy That Supports Recruitment & Retention
Cutting benefits sounds tempting, but it can backfire fast, especially in industries with high turnover or hiring challenges. Instead, restructure benefits to match what employees actually value.
Example:
Offer a lean core medical plan + optional extras through voluntary benefits.
Use a health reimbursement arrangement (HRA) to give flexibility without giving up control.
Consider adding or beefing up retirement plans and life insurance as they are WAY less expensive than a health plan and provide lasting, tangible monetary value for employees.
Final Thoughts
Tightening your belt doesn’t mean short-changing your employees or settling for worse care. It means being smarter about how you spend.

In a shaky economy, savings = strength. If you haven’t reviewed your health insurance strategy in the last 12 months, now’s the time. A few smart changes can free up thousands in cash flow without compromising on care.

title: Affordable Health Insurance for Small Businesses

blocks.text: Finding the Right Balance Between Cost and Coverage

Small businesses face an uphill battle when it comes to providing health insurance. Rising premiums, complex regulations, and a lack of affordable options leave many owners frustrated. But what if the problem isn’t just the cost, but how small businesses approach health benefits? Instead of sticking to the traditional playbook, it’s time to rethink coverage strategies to find solutions that are both affordable and effective.
Here’s how to make smarter choices when offering health benefits to your employees:
1. Stop Over-Insuring

Many small businesses buy coverage with low deductibles and rich benefits, thinking they’re doing right by their employees. But these plans come at a high price—often unnecessarily. Employees rarely use every benefit, meaning your business is paying for coverage that goes underutilized. Instead, focus on essential benefits that employees value most and structure plans in a way that reduces waste.
2. Stop Hating HMOs for No Reason

Many business owners avoid HMOs (Health Maintenance Organizations) because of outdated assumptions about poor networks or limited doctor choices. In reality, today’s HMOs offer robust networks and cost much less than traditional PPOs. By considering an HMO, you can reduce premiums without sacrificing quality care.
3. Look at ERISA Strategies

If your business has the right demographics—such as a younger and healthier workforce—you may be overpaying under ACA small group rules. ERISA-based strategies, like level-funded plans, allow businesses to lower costs because they can be customized and are priced more accurately to reflect the lower risk the group presents to the insurance company. These plans also offer the potential for refunds on unused claims dollars, something fully insured plans can’t provide.
4. Stop Focusing Only on Deductibles and Max Out-of-Pocket Costs

Most small businesses shop for health insurance based on two numbers: the deductible and max out-of-pocket. But the real cost driver isn’t just what employees pay when they get sick—it’s what your business pays in premiums every month. By looking deeper into cost structures, such as provider reimbursements and prescription costs, you can find ways to reduce premiums while still offering great coverage.
5. Maybe Cancel the Plan and Set Up an ICHRA

For some businesses, the best move is to ditch traditional group insurance altogether and switch to an Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement (ICHRA). ICHRAs let employees pick their own health plans, while employers set a budget that fits their needs. This approach gives employees more choices and can reduce employer costs.
6. If You’re a New Business, Consider Other High-Impact Benefits

If your business is just starting out, traditional health insurance may not be the best first investment. Other benefits—like company-paid life insurance, disability coverage, or a well-structured retirement plan—can provide meaningful financial security for employees at a fraction of the cost of a health plan. These benefits can help you attract and retain talent without breaking the bank.
The Bottom Line

Affordable health insurance isn’t about finding the cheapest plan—it’s about structuring benefits strategically. Whether it’s adjusting coverage levels, considering an HMO, exploring ERISA strategies, or even replacing traditional insurance with an ICHRA, small businesses have more options than they realize. The key is to think beyond the surface and focus on what really drives cost and value.

title: How Business Owners Become Their Own Bank

blocks.text: As a business owner, accessing capital can be a constant challenge. Traditional bank loans come with interest payments, strict lending requirements, and loss of financial control. But what if you could be your own bank? With Company-Owned Life Insurance (COLI), you can create a tax-advantaged funding source that gives you flexibility, liquidity, and financial security. Here’s how it works and why it might be a smart strategy for your business.
What is COLI?

Company-Owned Life Insurance (COLI) is a permanent life insurance policy that a business purchases on key employees or owners. The company owns the policy, pays the premiums, and is the beneficiary. The policy accumulates cash value over time, which can be accessed tax-efficiently - often as early as year 2.
How Can COLI Be Used Like a Bank?
Cash Value Accumulation: COLI policies build cash value that grows tax-deferred. This becomes a financial asset your business can leverage.

Tax-Free Loans: You can borrow against the cash value of the policy at favorable interest rates. Unlike traditional loans, these policy loans do not require credit approval and do not show up on your personal credit report.
No Loan Repayment Pressure: Unlike bank loans, policy loans do not have fixed repayment schedules. You can repay them on your terms or allow the loan balance to be deducted from the death benefit.
Tax-Efficient Withdrawals: In certain cases, cash value can be withdrawn tax-free up to the amount of premiums paid, providing liquidity without tax consequences.
Practical Uses of COLI for Business Owners
Financing Business Growth: Use policy loans to fund expansion, acquire new equipment, or invest in marketing without dealing with traditional lenders.
Emergency Fund: The cash value serves as a reserve for unexpected expenses or downturns.
Executive Compensation: COLI can be used to provide benefits to key employees, offering bonuses or deferred compensation.
Exit Planning & Buy-Sell Agreements: The policy’s death benefit ensures liquidity to fund buyouts of partners or protect against financial instability in the event of an owner’s passing.
Why COLI is a Better Alternative to Traditional Banking
Control: You control the borrowing process, repayment terms, and access to funds.
Tax Advantages: Tax-free growth, tax-free loans, and a tax-free death benefit provide significant advantages over conventional loans.
Asset Protection: In many states, the cash value of life insurance enjoys creditor protection, shielding business assets.
Guaranteed Liquidity: Unlike other business assets, COLI provides predictable and accessible cash when needed.
Comparing COLI Loans to Bank Loans
When deciding whether to borrow from a COLI policy or a bank, consider the differences:
Which One is Better?
COLI loans often have lower interest rates than bank loans, especially if the policy is structured properly.
Unlike banks, COLI does not require credit approval, making access to capital easier.
Policy loans allow cash value to continue growing, which can offset borrowing costs.
Bank loans may have lower rates for businesses with excellent credit, but they require strict repayment schedules and collateral.
Is COLI Right for You?

COLI is best suited for businesses with steady revenue that can afford to fund the policy over time. It requires careful planning, and working with an insurance professional is key to structuring the policy for maximum benefit.
Final Thoughts

Being your own bank through COLI can transform the way you finance your business. With tax advantages, liquidity, and financial security, it provides a strategic alternative to traditional lending. If you’re looking for a smarter way to manage cash flow, finance growth, and protect your business, COLI might be the perfect solution.

blocks.text: Your business is your most valuable asset, but what happens if an owner unexpectedly leaves, becomes incapacitated, or passes away? Without a plan in place, business continuity can be at risk, leading to financial strain, disputes, or even the dissolution of the company. This is where a buy/sell agreement proves its worth.
What Is a Buy/Sell Agreement?

A buy/sell agreement is a legally binding contract that outlines what happens to a business owner's share of the company in case of a triggering event, such as death, disability, retirement, or voluntary departure. By establishing clear terms, it ensures a smooth transition of ownership and minimizes disruptions to operations.
The Benefits of a Buy/Sell Agreement
1. Ensures Business Continuity
Without a structured plan, the sudden departure of an owner can create instability. A buy/sell agreement guarantees an orderly transition, keeping the business operational.
2. Prevents Ownership Disputes
Without predefined terms, disagreements can arise among remaining owners or heirs. A buy/sell agreement eliminates uncertainty by clearly outlining ownership transition rules.
3. Protects Financial Interests
A buy/sell agreement provides a method for valuing ownership stakes, ensuring a fair market price for both selling and remaining owners.
4. Provides Liquidity for Heirs or Departing Owners

If an owner passes away or exits the business, their family may need financial support. A buy/sell agreement—often funded by life or disability insurance—ensures they receive fair compensation while the business remains stable.
5. Restricts Ownership Transfers to Outside Parties
A buy/sell agreement ensures that shares stay within the business by granting existing owners the first right to purchase a departing partner’s share, preventing unwanted third-party involvement.
Common Buy/Sell Agreement Structures
Cross-Purchase Agreement: Allows remaining owners to buy the departing owner’s share.
Entity Purchase Agreement: The business itself repurchases the departing owner's shares.
Hybrid Agreement: Combines aspects of both cross-purchase and entity purchase agreements for added flexibility.
How to Set Up a Buy/Sell Agreement
Consult a Business Attorney – Work with a professional to draft an agreement tailored to your business needs.
Establish a Valuation Method – Define how ownership stakes will be valued.
Secure Funding Mechanisms – Life insurance or other financial strategies can ensure funds are available for buyouts.
Define Triggering Events – Clearly outline the circumstances under which the agreement takes effect.
Review and Update Periodically – Adjust the agreement as the business evolves.
Final Thoughts

A buy/sell agreement is an essential tool for business owners seeking stability, financial security, and a smooth transition plan. By putting one in place, entrepreneurs can ensure their business and legacy remain protected.

blocks.text: A Beginner’s Experience with Tax Reduction, Wealth Accumulation and Asset Protection

Owning a business is, financially speaking, the riskiest way to make a living. More business owners fail than succeed and if anything goes wrong, all your income and assets are at risk because you have everything in this one basket.

Properly structuring your compensation can significantly impact your tax liability and long-term financial growth. In this case study, we will explore the impacts on the two owners of an Arizona-based S-Corp earning $400,000 in profits each – comparing tax liabilities and showing how strategic planning can optimize financial outcomes.
Let’s look at the current compensation structure for each owner: 60% Wages, 40% Distribution
Compensation: Wages: $240,000 | Distributions: $160,000
Total Taxes: $128,864 (Includes federal, state, and FICA)
Remaining Cash and Investments: $271,136
Step One – Tax Savings and Wealth Accumulation

A slight increase to wages allows the owners to maximize pre-tax contributions to a SEP IRA which provides tax savings now for the business owners and allows tax-deferred growth while also being a powerful tool for wealth accumulation. The SEP contribution is subtracted from wages, lowering the overall tax obligation.
New Compensation Structure for each owner: $265K Wages, $135K Distribution, $69K SEP IRA Contribution
Compensation: Wages: $265,000 | Distributions: $135,000 | SEP IRA: $69,000
Total Taxes: $112,389 (Includes federal, state and FICA)
Cash and Investments: $287,611
This is over $16,000 in tax savings and additional wealth – for each of them – every year.
Assuming the S-Corp owners contribute this $69,000 annually for 10 years with the standard average market return of 10%, their anticipated value is $1,209,651.
After ten years, if the S-Corp owners decide to stop investing for some reason, the accumulated returns would continue to grow and by age 60, the accounts would each be worth almost $9,000.000,00.
However, there are no guarantees regarding market returns and there will be tax consequences once the owners start withdrawing their money.
Step Two – More Tax Savings, Wealth Accumulation and Asset Protection

To mitigate the risk associated with investing and provide increased asset protection, a $4,500,000 Indexed Universal Life (IUL) policy is added. It is funded over ten years and provides tax-advantaged growth and tax-free access to funds later.

With an IUL, policyholders benefit from principal protection (never losing money due toa market downturns) while still participating in market-linked growth. Though also not guaranteed, the policy’s value could realistically grow to more than $10,000,000.00.
They can also access this money tax-free making the IUL a great way to counter the potential future tax liabilities from the SEP or, it could be designed as a tax-free pension.
Now, each owner has created a minimum legacy for their families of nearly $20,000,000.00.
Step Three – Buy/Sell Agreement
Lastly, there needs to be protection for each owner’s business interest in the event tragedy strikes. Currently the company is valued at $1,000,000.00.

A buy/sell agreement is put in place backed by a term life insurance policy. This is used to fund the purchase of the business, so no one has to worry about securing loans or selling personal assets to buy out the other owner’s estate. The insurance does this for us and we will have to update the policy every few years to reflect the increase in the value of the business as it grows.
What if My Company Is Not This Big?

Size truly does not matter. Any business owner can use these strategies. The amounts, investments and insurance products are simply scaled to fit the situation. In fact, it is better to start earlier because your money has longer to grow thanks to compound interest.
In the example above, had the owners started five years earlier with smaller amounts, their financial legacies would be estimated nearly 30% higher than their current projection.
Conclusion: The First Steps Toward A Financial Legacy
Though owning a business is financially risky, properly structuring compensation and sound planning can mitigate the risks.

S-Corp owners have a lot of different options available to them and whether the goal is reducing current tax burdens, accumulating long-term wealth, or securing assets, there is a strategy that can ensure financial stability in both the short and long term.

Taking the right steps early can make all the difference. If you’d like a personalized plan tailored to your business and financial goals, let’s discuss which strategies can work for you! business owner financial planning

blocks.text: When it comes to planning, small business owners often focus on cash flow, taxes, and employee benefits. But one often-overlooked strategy that impacts them all is Company-Owned Life Insurance (COLI).
What is COLI?

Company-Owned Life Insurance (COLI) is a policy purchased by a business on the lives of key employees, including owners. The company pays the premiums and is the beneficiary of the policy, meaning it receives the death benefit when the insured individual passes away. These policies can also accumulate cash value over time, providing financial flexibility.
Key Benefits of COLI for Small Business Owners
1. Business Continuity & Succession Planning

If a key employee or owner passes away unexpectedly, a COLI policy provides a death benefit that can help the business stay afloat. It ensures that surviving partners or family members have the funds to cover expenses, repay debts, or buy out shares from an estate.
2. Tax Advantages

Although the premiums cannot be deducted because the company is the beneficiary, the cash value growth of a COLI policy is tax-deferred. Additionally, the death benefit is generally tax-free to the business, providing a significant financial cushion.
3. Lowering Employee Turnover

Many COLI policies can be structured to fund executive compensation programs, such as deferred compensation or retirement benefits. This can be a great way to retain top talent by offering long-term financial incentives.
4. Becoming Your Own Bank

Over time, the COLI policy builds up cash value that the business can record as an asset. The company can borrow against or use this asset for future investments, expansions, or even emergency funding. You can sidestep traditional banking and access money without an approval process and usually at lower interest rates.
5. Funding Buy-Sell Agreements
For businesses with multiple owners, COLI can be used to fund buy-sell agreements, ensuring that the remaining owners can purchase the deceased owner’s shares without depleting company reserves.
Is COLI Right for Your Business?
If you’re a small business owner looking to strengthen your company’s financial foundation while protecting key stakeholders, COLI might be a smart addition to your business strategy.

title: Rich Person's Roth: The High Earner's Tax-Free Wealth Strategy

blocks.text: No one likes paying taxes, especially high earners who see a significant portion of their income disappearing to federal and state obligations. While there are multiple ways to achieve tax-free growth, one of the most efficient and high-impact strategies is leveraging permanent life insurance as a "Rich Person’s Roth."
What is the Rich Person’s Roth?

The term "Rich Person’s Roth" refers to strategies that allow high-income earners to benefit from tax-free growth, even when they exceed Roth IRA income limits. Also referred to as "Infinite Banking", cash-value life insurance provides the most "bang for the buck" when it comes to long-term, tax-free wealth accumulation.
Using Permanent Life Insurance for Tax-Free Wealth Growth

For high earners who have maxed out traditional retirement accounts, cash-value life insurance policies—such as whole life or indexed universal life (IUL)—offer an effective alternative to Roth accounts.
How It Works:
Premium Contributions: You pay premiums into a permanent life insurance policy, with part of the payment going toward the death benefit and part accumulating as cash value.
Tax-Deferred Growth: The cash value grows over time without being taxed, similar to a Roth IRA.
Tax-Free Access: You can take loans or withdrawals from the cash value without incurring income taxes. This is "Infinite Banking" because you are creating a self-sustaining financial system.
No Contribution Limits: Unlike Roth IRAs, which have strict income and contribution limits, cash-value policies have no such restrictions.
No Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs): Unlike a Roth 401(k), life insurance policies do not require withdrawals at a certain age.
Key Benefits of This Strategy

Tax-Free Income in Retirement: By taking policy loans instead of withdrawals, you avoid taxation while still accessing your accumulated wealth. You can essentially create a pension for yourself, if you want.
Asset Protection: Depending on your state, life insurance policies may offer creditor protection, safeguarding wealth from lawsuits or financial liabilities.
Legacy Planning: The death benefit is paid out tax-free to beneficiaries, making this an attractive tool for estate planning.
Flexibility: Unlike retirement accounts, which impose early withdrawal penalties, life insurance cash value can be accessed at any time without penalties.
Who Should Consider This Strategy?
This approach works best for individuals who:
Have maxed out their 401(k) and other tax-advantaged retirement options.
Are high-income earners looking to minimize taxes.
Want tax-free income in retirement without RMDs.
Need a flexible, long-term wealth accumulation vehicle with estate planning benefits.
Final Thoughts

While there are many strategies for achieving tax-free wealth, leveraging permanent life insurance as a "Rich Person’s Roth" provides a powerful combination of tax efficiency, flexibility, and long-term financial security. If you’re looking to shield your wealth from taxes and build a financial legacy, exploring a properly structured permanent life insurance policy is a smart move.

title: THE BIG REASON YOU'RE OVERPAYING FOR YOUR COMPANY HEALTH PLAN
description: Most insurance coverage is priced based on the risk you represent to the insurance company.

blocks.text: Most insurance coverage is priced based on the risk you represent to the insurance company.
Have a lot of workplace accidents? You pay more for worker’s compensation coverage.
Have employees that are safe drivers? You pay less for vehicle coverage.
But health insurance, that is very different.

Are your employees healthy and rarely go to the doctor? You get to PAY THE SAME AMOUNT as a company of SOFAPOTAMUSES where everyone is 100 pounds overweight and has high blood pressure, coronary artery disease and diabetes.
WHY YOU ARE OVERPAYING AND WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT
You are overpaying because you are using small business ACA priced plans that determine premiums based on your geographic location instead of your group’s actual health needs.
Plans that price based on health needs fall under ERISA law and the most common option for small businesses is to use a “level-funded” health plan.

Level-funded health plans set premiums based on actual health needs as determined by confidential questionnaires filled out by your employees. If your group is healthy or does not use medical care often, rates can be much lower for the same comprehensive PPO plan you’re already using.
WHAT’S THE CATCH?

The catch is that it is different. The different components of a health insurance plan are managed by just one company when you use ACA plans. Level-funded plans are usually a combination of different providers.
DOES IT EVER GO WRONG?

Absolutely! Level-funded plans are priced based on the insurance company’s best guess of how much medical care your group will need for the year. The good news is that if they guess wrong and charge too much (meaning the plan was not used very much), then they will provide a refund of overpaid premiums to the business.
That’s right. THEY WILL PROVIDE A REFUND. And the average refund in 2022 was over $8,0001

If they underpriced it, you would NOT have to pay more. They will however raise your rates the next year but, you are not forced to renew the plan. If the rate increase is too steep, you can always switch back to an ACA plan and this is the strategy a lot of small businesses use to keep their costs as low as possible for as long as possible.
IF THIS IS SO GREAT, WHY HAVEN’T I HEARD ABOUT IT OR WHY DOESN’T EVERYONE USE IT?

Well, actually, about 40% already do use this option2. If you have not heard about it, it is possible your broker is just not familiar with it. This is just a guess, but we make it because the insurance industry suffers from very high turnover and most agents/brokers quit within five years. It’s just possible your broker hasn’t been around long enough.
Obviously, this is only an introduction to level-funded health plans. If you would like to know more or perhaps look deeper at this option for your business, don’t be shy, reach out to us.

blocks.text: Offering health insurance is one of the most valuable benefits a small business can provide employees, helping attract and retain top talent while ensuring a healthier workforce. However, choosing the right health plan can be overwhelming, especially with the variety of options available.
If you're a small business owner looking to provide health benefits without breaking the bank, here’s a guide to the best types of health plans that balance cost, flexibility, and coverage.
1. ICHRA (Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement)
Best for: Small businesses that want flexibility and cost control

An ICHRA allows businesses to reimburse employees for individual health insurance plans instead of offering a traditional group plan. This approach enables employees to choose coverage that suits their needs while allowing employers to set a budget without worrying about premium increases.
Why Small Businesses Like ICHRA:

✔ Cost Control: Employers set their reimbursement amount, making it easier to manage expenses.
✔ Employee Choice: Workers can pick the plan that works best for them.
✔ Avoids Group Plan Requirements: No need to meet participation or contribution requirements.
✔ Tax Benefits: Reimbursements are tax-free for employees and deductible for employers.
Ideal for: Small businesses with diverse employee needs or those struggling with high group plan costs.
2. Level-Funded Health Plans
Best for: Businesses with healthy employees looking for savings

A level-funded plan is a type of self-funded health plan where employers pay a fixed monthly amount that covers claims, administrative fees, and stop-loss insurance (protection against high claims). If claims are lower than expected, the business gets a refund at the end of the year.
Why Small Businesses Like Level-Funded Plans:

✔ Potential Savings: If claims are lower than projected, you receive money back.
✔ More Affordable than ACA Small Group Plans: Companies with younger, healthier employees often save significantly.
✔ ERISA Advantage: These plans are regulated under ERISA rather than the ACA, offering more flexibility.
Ideal for: Companies with younger, healthier employees who want an alternative to traditional small-group plans.
3. High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) with an HRA
Best for: Businesses that want cost savings while providing richer benefits for employees

A High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) with a Health Reimbursement Arrangement (HRA) is a strategic way for small businesses to save money while still offering strong benefits. Instead of just shifting costs to employees, the business provides an HRA to reimburse some or all of the out-of-pocket costs, making the plan feel more like a traditional health plan with lower employee costs.
Why Small Businesses Like HDHPs with HRAs:

✔ Lower Premiums: HDHPs cost less than traditional group health plans.
✔ Employer-Controlled Reimbursement: Employers decide how much to contribute to the HRA.
✔ Better Employee Benefits: Employees get reimbursement for deductibles and medical expenses, reducing their financial burden.
✔ Tax Benefits: Employer contributions are tax-deductible, and reimbursements are tax-free for employees.
Ideal for: Businesses that want lower premium costs but also want to offer competitive benefits without shifting too much cost to employees.
4. Traditional Small Group Health Insurance (Fully Insured Plans)
Best for: Businesses that want a simple, predictable option
A fully insured plan is the most common health insurance option, where the business pays a set monthly premium to an insurance company. The insurer then takes on the risk of paying employees’ claims.
Why Small Businesses Like Fully Insured Plans:

✔ Predictable Costs: No unexpected claims expenses.
✔ Easy to Administer: The insurance company handles most of the work.
✔ No Financial Risk: Unlike level-funded plans, there’s no risk of losing money on claims.
Ideal for: Small businesses that prefer a straightforward, hands-off approach to employee health coverage.
5. High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) with a Health Savings Account (HSA)
Best for: Cost-conscious businesses and employees who want tax benefits

A High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) has lower monthly premiums but higher out-of-pocket costs. Employees can pair it with a Health Savings Account (HSA), where they save money tax-free for medical expenses.
Why Small Businesses Like HDHPs with HSAs:

✔ Lower Premiums: More affordable monthly costs compared to traditional plans.
✔ Tax Advantages: Employees and employers can contribute tax-free funds to the HSA.
✔ Employee Ownership: The HSA belongs to the employee, even if they leave the company.
Ideal for: Small businesses that want to lower costs while offering employees a way to save for medical expenses.
6. Professional Employer Organization (PEO) Health Plans
Best for: Businesses that want to outsource HR functions and access large-group health insurance rates

A Professional Employer Organization (PEO) is a company that acts as a co-employer for small businesses, handling HR functions like payroll, compliance, and benefits administration. By joining a PEO, small businesses can access large-group health insurance rates, often at a lower cost than traditional small-group plans.
Why Small Businesses Like PEOs:

✔ Lower Premiums: PEOs pool multiple small businesses together to get better insurance rates.
✔ Less Administrative Work: The PEO handles compliance, payroll, and benefits, reducing the burden on business owners.
✔ More Comprehensive Benefits: Employees may get access to better coverage than they could with a small-group plan.
Ideal for: Small businesses that want to offer competitive benefits but don’t have the time or resources to manage HR and insurance administration.
